utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber intends today to sit for the whole of the day, as was said before, and that we would stop for the morning at quarter past one and would restart quarter past two, so have one hour for lunch break so that we effectively would have seven and a half hours today. If possible the Chamber would very much like to see whether we could finish with this witness today, since I am not available tomorrow. Madam Usher could you please escort Mr. Pasic into the courtroom, unless there is something to be raised at the moment, Mr. Josse. If there is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. I further would like to inform you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would further like to inform you that, not as usual, we are not just sitting the morning or an afternoon but we will sit for the whole of the day so it will be a very long day for you as well. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness have the bundle of documents placed in front of him, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We were examining, Mr. Pasic, various aspects of tab 1, the Crisis Staff report, when we adjourned last night. Can I ask you this question about that document? Did you personally provide it to the Defence, either lawyers, investigators, anything along those lines? If you don't remember, say so.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't provide them with this document. I don't think that I gave the document to the investigators but I did tell the investigators that there were certain documents at the municipal building, not only relating to the war. I didn't know exactly what was there and what wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we were examining the history of this document, and I think by looking at tab 1 and tab 2, we are going to be able to accomplish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- if we are dealing with more tabs, then I would like Mr. Registrar to assign an exhibit number to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 1, Your Honours, will be D115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the report on the work of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dealing with tab 1 just for a moment longer, if we look at the very first paragraph, which I'm going to go through in a little bit more detail in moment or two's time because that really relates to Judge Hanoteau's question which started very helpfully this matter off, we can see, can't we, in the second or third line that it says the Crisis Staff was set up at the beginning of April, on the very first page, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we then look at the -- towards the end of the document, we can see, I think on the last page, that it says, paragraph -- about the middle of the page, there is something like this: This analysis, the work of the Crisis Staff in the municipality, its inception and chronology of all events in the past two and a half months shows, et cetera. Important words there, being in the past two and a half months. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then, if we go to tab 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I need to explain something about tab 2. Tab 2 has in fact already been exhibited. It's D15, as I understand it. That should be perhaps be added to the exhibit description list, front page of this bundle. The translation that's been provided is as follows: In fact, it speaks for itself on the face of the English document. We have described it as an unofficial translation of D15. It was exhibited on the 1st of June 2004, Court can see the transcript page, and what presumably happened - of course, it was long before I was here - was that when it was put to a particular witness by -- I think it was Ms. Loukas, the Court I assumed asked Ms. Cmeric to translate it. That she has done and I don't think it has ever been officially translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that she read it and it was then translated by the interpreters as part of the transcript. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much, Your Honour. It's extremely grammatical so it's -- it's a very helpful translation, but if we could deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll ask you to tell us more about it later, Mr. Pasic. We see, don't we, that it says, second -- somewhere near the top of the text of the document is as follows: Pursuant to Article 186, et cetera, of the Bosanski Novi Official Gazette, held on the 16th of June 1992. So this is in relation to a meeting that was held on the 16th of June 1992, number 1, the report on the work of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi is hereby adopted. And the conclusions, orders, and other decisions it reached are hereby confirmed. So would you agree that almost certainly this particular decision is referring to the report that we find in tab 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you may have noticed that I was very much not concentrating on what you said at this moment. The Registrar just provided me with what seems to be a normal translation of D15.1 so it does exist. Perhaps it could be -- if it would assist you, then it could be provided to you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think what I'll do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll deal with this now. I'll then turn back to this document later and I'll have it copied. I'll have 12 copies made right now so, if I may. If it can be provided to Mr. Sladojevic he'll go and do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, do you follow my question, Mr. Pasic? It appears, does it, that the report being referred to is the one that we've been examining?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have been following your question. I understand it. Tab 1 is the report on the work of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi and it was prepared for this meeting, and when you read the complete report chronologically then you can see that the actions described are for the period of May and part of June, up until mid-June, and you can see here that on the 16th of June, a meeting was held of the municipal assembly which reviewed the work of the Crisis Staff and it adopted a conclusion which is then contained here in tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's then go back, if we may, to tab 1, and analyse this report in a little bit more detail. And if we could have a look at the first paragraph, it explains, does it not, exactly why the Crisis Staff was set up? I'm bound to say the official translation unrevised that we have has -- the translator had some difficulty with the first sentence, so could I ask you slowly, please, to read out the very first sentence of the body of the document? Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its original form, the municipal Crisis Staff was formed at the beginning of April by the municipal board of the Serbian Democratic Party on the proposal and according to instructions of higher organs of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And it goes on to describe how the Crisis Staff was originally a political and operative body, how it worked, and what its initial aim was. Would that be an accurate summary of the first two or three sentences?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, there are a few other parts of this document that I would like to take you to because in many ways it reflects the point in your evidence that you had got to when this particular document was introduced. In the second paragraph, in your version on page 1, in the English translation on page 2, it says, "It was agreed that our opinions and policies should be clear and uniform and that no differing factions, soft and hard line, which did appear at certain moments, president of the municipal assembly versus the SDS leadership, were to be allowed." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It goes on to say that there had to be constant talks with the representatives of the SDA in search of a peaceful solution. Can I ask you what you understood the document to mean when it said the words in brackets, "President of the municipal assembly versus the SDS leadership"? What was that referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday evening that this report was written. I didn't personally draft it. It was an assessment, I think. On one page of the report it says that the person was the secretary of the municipal assembly of Novi Grad. Let me just find the page. His name is Djordje Pravuljac. I think he actually drafted the report because he was in charge of information and some kind of propaganda. You can see that on page 5, the list of people who were in charge of the different sectors, who were supposed to be doing what, and I think that this was something that he remarked on because it would happen that a number of people in the party itself, I repeat some people within the party, believed that somethings needed to be done faster in order to prevent any kind of unexpected situations. Others, however, felt that there had to be a more liberal or slower approach. I don't think that there was anything special or particular in this part, if I can say the way it's written here. In parentheses, the president of the assembly versus the SDS leadership. Of course, it was normal to discuss every problem but there were no divergences and I'm now thinking of the municipal leadership and the municipal SDS. Their positions didn't differ all that much. There was harmonisation, agreements reached, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next part I want to take you to is, I think, probably on page 2 of your original document. And, in fact, it is a clear translation error in the English. Bottom of page 2, in the English, it says, "In early May [4th of May 1991.]" If we look at the B/C/S version, it's clearly 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my copy it says 1992. I don't know what you have in yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And it says that concrete discussions begun with the SDA representatives regarding current political and security situation. Could you tell us anything more about those concrete discussions? I see you're very sensibly reading on to the end of the sentence. I will read it out for the record. It says "the position of the SRBH and its jurisdiction and disarmament, the SDA representatives pointed out that they would accept the SRBH as a transitional solution before final agreement on BH was reached. Its laws would have to be observed. As far as disarmament was concerned, all the people unlawfully armed would have to be disarmed regardless of ethnicity, and all the time involvement of the SDA in arming of Muslims was denied. This statement was not accepted by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We talked with the representatives from the highest leadership of the SDA political party. When I say the SDA political party I'm thinking of the municipal leaders of the SDA, not those at the republican level. We are talking about the municipal level where we discussed the current political and security situation which, as I said yesterday evening, was already tense and full of turmoil, and I would like to say that already conflicts had broken out in the area of Novi Grad municipality, war was already going on in Bosanski Novi, as well as on the other side, in the municipality of Prijedor. So we were in an environment where actually there was peace in a way, while war was waging all around us. We did try to find the strength to see what was in our common interest because we were living together in that area. So we wanted to make an assessment of the security situation with the SDA representatives. The position was the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina already existed and its jurisdiction, as it states here, had to be respected. The laws were literally transferred from the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina there. At least in the very beginning we stressed that all paramilitary formations which were creating enormous problems for us, and I think I gave some examples for that yesterday evening, we asked that everything, regardless of the ethnic groups or political orientation, be disarmed. This is where we sought the support of the SDA party and we had certain information through the public security station that some people from the democratic action party were arming illegally the Muslim part of the population, and we asked them, and we also asked the Serbian Democratic Party also to act amongst the Serbs and that the SDA is active amongst the Muslim or the Bosniak population because, as I repeat, these two people lived in the area of the Novi Grad municipality together. So I repeat, in that conversation, this was actually transcribed here more or less how the conversation proceeded. They pretended in a way that they didn't know anything about the arming and that they helped in this arming of the Muslim part of the population. I repeat, this information was something that we received from the public security station and, based on that information that a part of the Muslim population was armed, we actually asked the party to exert an influence over them and to try to have that part of the population, both the Muslim and Serb part of the population, disarmed and to place the weapons under the control of the TO Staff, and this was repeated several times. Actually, the representatives of the Muslim ethnic group refused to be mobilised. I said that -- in 1991 and even then we were suggesting that they should join the Territorial Defence Staff so that we would together with respect and in a way we would create security when the representatives of the Muslim ethnic group were part of the TO Staff. If they were mobilised to that staff then we would simply create a feeling of security amongst the Muslim people, too, by the TO. They still continued to refuse to be mobilised and, as I said, they pretended not to know anything about these weapons and I think it says here in the last sentence, in this passage, that the statement was not accepted by the Crisis Staff. I think that was the reason why this was written in this way. This denial on their part about the existence of weapons and that there was no influence exerted by them on these paramilitary groups, that is why I think this sentence was written the way it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The report continues dealing with the matter in some detail, does it not, at page 3 in the B/C/S version, page 4 in the English version, where it talks about, the paragraph that begins in English, "regarding the implementation of the government's decision on disarming, 5th of May, Crisis Staff representatives invested a lot of effort in negotiations with the SDA representatives in order to implement the disarming action peacefully. Crisis Staff session was held after every meeting to assess what was achieved on negotiations. SDA representatives always demonstrated their readiness to implement this action successfully. However, it turned out that either they had little influence on Muslim people or they were remarkably perfidious, saying one thing on the negotiations and then something completely different to their members. However, at the deadline, 11th of May, 1500 hours, a small quantity of armaments was surrendered." Does that jog your recollection about how the matter developed really up to the outbreak of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of that question, "after the outbreak of hostilities" is very imprecise because I understood that the outbreak of hostilities started on the 11th of May and there were no hostilities prior to that time. So I'm not sure what counsel is referring to. I would ask him to clarify that portion of his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly what my learned friend just said, up to the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found the paragraph. However, it seems to me that it wasn't translated into Serbian as it says here. Things seem to have -- some words seem to have been turned around in the translation. Can we read -- well, I don't know where to start. It says, a staff meeting was held to analyse what was achieved in the talks and every time the representatives of the SDA expressed their readiness to succeed in the action. However, it turned out that they either had little influence on the Muslim people or they were going along two tracks. That is to say, saying one thing in the negotiations and doing something different with their members. However, by the deadline of the 11th of May, and then it says -- 1500 hours, very small quantities of arms were surrendered but those quantities meant a recognition of the legitimacy of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their organs. Now, if I've understood the question correctly, what is being attempted here is to describe the situation up until that date, the 11th of May, and here it says, that in or rather in the previous part it says that the meeting took place on the 4th of May. I don't think that all the many meetings that we had with the representatives of the SDA were included in the Crisis Staff meetings because I went to work every day myself, for instance, and usually during the day I would be in contact either on the phone or personally in my office with people from the SDA party and people from the SDS party in an attempt to try and see what we could do in each situation and try to prevent anything that would lead to war, the outbreak of war. So I think that this is just one segment that has been described, just one of the ways that all this happened, and perhaps let me repeat that an observation would be in order, when this report was written, how it depicted an image. Perhaps a subjective one, a subjective opinion, in describing the reactions, whether they it any influence on the Muslim people or did not or whether they simply worked along these two lines, this double track, whether they were bluffing. So the dilemma remains with this written report as to what the real truth of it was and what the true image was that the representatives of the SDA party portrayed. So I think that in this text, the way it's been written is that there was a dilemma as to what their true position was, given a situation and the point in time that they found themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next passage that I'd invite you to look at is -- I think probably at page 3, the last paragraph on that page in your version, page 5 in the English. And it's towards the bottom of the page. It says, "Simultaneously with the armed conflict, certain groups of people are engaging in looting which can't be prevented or controlled. Various armed groups are arriving and are introducing themselves as regular units, military police and so on, when in fact they operate under no control or command and are engaging in looting activities." I can see that you've got that. Tell us about your recollection of the looting, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I said last night something about these events, and unfortunately if we have understood the role of the Crisis Staff, that quite literally it provided suggestions and that it was a group of people in certain positions and this can be seen here in several places, that means that we, during our daily contacts and the talks we had with the chief of the public security station, the command of the TO, we really did indicate these very great problems that we were facing. But they said to us that it was almost or well-nigh impossible that throughout the territory of the Novi Grad municipality, to effect control and to prevent such incidents from taking place such as looting on the part of certain groups who even wore some sort of uniform or different uniforms at that time because there were, of course, different uniforms that were worn here and there, people from certain military units who either earlier or -- were created either earlier or at that point in time, and some people even introduced themselves falsely. They gave false identities, groups would, say, change into camouflage uniform and put a white belt over their uniforms which -- to denote the military police. The military police had these white belts, so we did have instances in which these people quite literally attacked private property and worked within that context, contrary to the law, and they were indeed crimes that took place. But let me repeat what the Crisis Staff could do was that it could just launch an appeal to the police station and the TO headquarters to try and prevent such untoward behaviour. And let me repeat, we did receive information from the commander of the TO as we did indeed from the chief of the public security station but it was practically impossible to control all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in this regard I'm going to jump forward in the report a little bit and then go back. At the bottom of page 5 in the B/C/S version, bottom of page 8 in the English, page 5 in your version, Mr. Pasic, the report -- dealing with the period towards the end of May, it says, "The order was not followed through which led to complete chaos. The villages mentioned, which were Muslim villages about which we are going to hear a little bit later, were completely looted and enormous problems appeared in relation to civilian defence. There were men killed, many houses were set on fire, as well as other structures, many livestock carcasses were either killed during looting or perished through bloating," and then it goes on and deals with matters of hygiene, sanitation and the threat of an epidemic. Now, I don't think you had got to that point in your evidence yesterday. What is that referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find that passage but I haven't found it yet, what you've just read out. Did you say page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the very bottom --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's the last four words in B/C/S on page 5, and then it continues on to page 6.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the last sentence on page 5 that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The order was not adhered to." Yes. Well, this describes a period which would be, if I've understood it correctly, to be the end of May, the last third of May, which was when there was a crisis, if you look at it as time, and the Crisis Staff really did endeavour, and yes, property was destroyed, cattle had died, and the situation was as it says here, the hygienic situation and the threat of epidemics breaking out, so we asked the civilian protection staff to undertake certain measures in order to try and prevent that from happening, and I've just read a sentence, I don't know whether you read that one out, but it says here that teams went out into the field but were not able to work normally because they were shot at, and so was the police shot at. So I think these teams that tried to deal with the perished livestock and tried to bury them to prevent any epidemics from taking place, that these paramilitaries that were responsible for the unrest targeted the civilian police, and the team. They shot at them. And perhaps I ought to mention that the paramilitary units did shoot at these people. They really did. And there was some sabotage going on, and it mentions the digger used to bury the cattle, the livestock. There is an explanation given so that the deputies in the assembly should get the proper picture of what was going on during that period of time. We tried to explain the kind of problems we were encountering, many problems involving these paramilitaries. So we weren't even able to bury the carcasses of the livestock that had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understood correctly, you were talking about a particularly chaotic period. Before the beginning, before this chaotic period started, I would like to know who was in charge of maintaining peace? How many people were there involved before the conflict? How was the police organised? The Territorial Defence as well in that municipality? You were the president of the municipality so you must know what is the number of the regular forces, how many people were involved? You were talking to us about paramilitaries, about various groups. But how was law and order maintained and by whom? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, public law and order, as I said, was maintained by the regular police force. That is to say, the public security station, as we called it. That was the term that we inherited from the social system of the former Yugoslavia. The regular police force was in charge of preserving law and order and that came under the exclusive competence of them and to whom I told you to whom the police was responsible. The chief of the public security station or commander was appointed by the Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example. So that was that chain of command and responsibility. And I said there were contacts both by telephone and in other waist although it wasn't actually my responsibility either to issue orders or to provide the public security station -- I mean, I could make suggestions but I didn't have the authority to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interrupting you because I just wanted to know how many men were involved in the maintenance of law and order of that municipality. Were we talking about a thousand people, a thousand men, a hundred men? Ten men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in the public security station, there were a total of about 60 policemen. But don't hold me to the figure. I think it was roughly that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what would happen in a situation of a disaster, for instance, or another conflict? The Territorial Defence was to maintain law and order in your municipality? Was that also one of their roles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Territorial Defence was a military formation and its task in a way was that, but for well-known reasons and the extraordinary situation that reigned when the war broke out, they did have the role, the military role, more than the public security station did, preserving law and order and excessive behaviour. So I think that there we had a division of competence for misdemeanours and lower scale crimes, then it would be the security station that would act. If there were more serious instances and violations, then it would be the military, if it surpassed the capabilities of the public security station, if it didn't have enough men to deal with the situation. Now, when we speak about paramilitaries and paramilitary units, then probably it would be the Territorial Defence Staff that would be in charge of suppressing any untoward behaviour rather than the others, if I've understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Last question, Witness: There is always a beginning and an end, of course. At the very beginning, things changed suddenly. Do you know if there were some arrests made immediately by those 60 police officers? Did they try to -- did they attempt to arrest people? Did they do what they were supposed to do? Did they do the necessary --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although those operational matters, I cannot say specifically or give you any names but I do know when this report was written, when we had meetings with the chief of the public security station, he did inform us about cases of that kind. Of course, there were certain arrests and the law courts went into action. There were cases like that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are two other points in this document I'd like to ask you about. Could we go back in your version to the last paragraph on page 4? And in the English, towards the top of page 7, where it says, "With a slight delay, the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have forwarded instructions for the work of municipal Crisis Staffs. Our municipality received the instructions on 20 May and in accordance with the instructions we have immediately approached the reorganisation of the Crisis Staff." And then it goes on and deals with those in a little bit of detail. Do you have any recollection as to these instructions, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't remember the details. I can't be precise. But roughly speaking, I do know what this refers to, the instructions. Although judging by the instructions, the Crisis Staff, and I think I said something about that last night, did not work or was not working because there was no need for it to be established earlier on. It says here the beginning of April. Now, whether it was the beginning or not or the middle of the month it's difficult to say now what the exact period was. The Crisis Staff therefore did not have, as it says here, and there is no reason for me not to believe it, that it actually happened on the 20th of May, that is to say when the unfortunate events had already broken out, and, as a human being, I was affected by the fact that we had no, absolutely no, information coming into us from the competent republican organs as to how we could try to stop the war and prevent these unfortunate events from taking place because quite simply nobody gave us any -- well, instructions or guidelines. We were left to fend for ourselves at the local municipal level, to do what we could, and to try to solve the problems ourselves. So that was what hit me hard personally, because I was left to fend for myself, to deal with the situation with my associates, as it says here, who were in the Crisis Staff, to deal with every situation as it arose, to try and find the best possible solution for any event and to try to prevent any escalation which went along the lines of destruction of property and people, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The final part of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question? You have now repeatedly told us that Crisis Staff, was no need to be active. Are you now talking about -- because we were at that portion of the report which says something about the 20th of May, do you mean to say that the Crisis Staff, that there was no -- as a matter of fact, no need to operate before that 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we read this report chronologically, then it gives a picture that is incomplete. We see here that the Crisis Staff, and I've already said this, the public security station, the TO staff and so on, the people who were at the meetings and working together at the meetings, that Crisis Staff, as it says, existed from the month of April. It did exist. But let me repeat, it did not work according to any instructions. It would meet, convene, and it called itself, gave itself the title and name of "Crisis Staff." And you'll see that this was pursuant to a former law of Bosnia and Herzegovina by which a council existed. So that was the council in actual fact that was composed of individuals who performed functions by virtue of the posts they held so that this Crisis Staff was in fact that council for national defence, as it existed in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina and as it was provided for by the law and by the Statute. So it did exist, yes, the Crisis Staff did exist before the 20th of May. However, it was not given any instructions and guidelines governing its work in any strict form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- you said two minutes ago -- and I think I said something about that last night, that "Crisis Staff did not work or was not working because there was no need for it to be established earlier on." Which period did you have in mind? Did you have in mind the period until the 20th of May? When exactly do you think that there was any need for the Crisis Staff to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I meant was the period before the month of April 1992. That is to say quite simply there was no need up until mid-April 1992 for the Crisis Staff to exist. I wasn't thinking of up to the 20th of May. I was thinking of mid-April to the 20th of May when the Crisis Staff was in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So once it was established, there was a need for the Crisis Staff to work? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand your question. The need for what existed? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The need for a Crisis Staff to be established because there was work to be done by such a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I already emphasised that the need arose as of mid-April. When the situation around Novi Grad was heated, when the war started we became conscious of the situation we were facing so it was at that time that it began working, or, rather, that the Crisis Staff was given a role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. That certainly clarifies my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So as I say, the last part of this report that I want to ask you about really leads on to the -- what is going to amount to the second part of your testimony, and this can be found at page 6 in the B/C/S version, page 9 in the English, and really it's immediately after the description of the looting and killings that took place at various Muslim villages. I'll read out the paragraph. "The population in Blagaj remained without a solution, so one was requested for its migration. Negotiations were held with the organs of the autonomous region, with the government of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and UNPROFOR. The remaining possibility was to expedite a voluntary emigration towards Banja Luka and that a return to the valley of Japra was definitely impossible but this population showed no willingness for it." Now, I think the first thing you should perhaps explain, Mr. Pasic, I don't think you've done so, I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, is the geographical area that this refers to when it talks about the population of Blagaj. Where was it in Bosanski Novi and how many villages did it involve? What sort of size of population, what were their ethnicity, this sort of matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you're aware that we received already quite some evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am aware, Your Honour. If the Court is happy with the background, then I'm content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the valley that goes north-south, which ends at the northern part in Blagaj where there was a railway section east-west et cetera. That's all in evidence and even without looking at my papers or even without having reread them it's clearly in my mind and I see that the same is true for my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That makes -- I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then really all I want you to deal with, Mr. Pasic, is where the Crisis Staff and/or the municipal assembly for this purpose were up to, so far as these people were concerned at the time of the writing of this report, clearly in early to mid-June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? The Crisis Staff what? You mean what was the role of the Crisis Staff in this situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It wasn't a very good question. It wasn't remotely precise enough. My apologies. At the point that this report was written, what were the municipal authorities collectively hoping to achieve in relation to the population of Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal leadership was literally placed before a fait accompli. It didn't have the option of choosing what to do. What happened was what was described, that in the Japra valley, that part from Blagaj to the valley all the way up to Gornji Alagici, we were explaining that earlier, that's an area inhabited by the Muslim population and what happened was that these paramilitary formations committed certain, let me say, crimes which moved the population in the direction of the village of Blagaj. We tried to get some kind of order established so that these people could return home. When we came to the Japra valley, we talked with some of the deputies from the SDA party who asked me if they could leave that area. I think that you can see that in this last sentence here, when it says that the population did not show any willingness for that to return to the valley of Japra, and we are talking about some villages which are higher up from Blagaj, Crna Rijeka, Suhaca, Hodzici, Agici. People from those villages had come down to this settlement called Blagaj. So this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you here for one moment? You just said, "When we came to Japra valley we talked with some of the deputies from the SDA party, who asked me if they could leave that area." I think that you can see that in the last sentence here, when it says that "a population did not show any willingness for that return." Let's now read the last line of this paragraph, which says, "The remaining possibility was to expedite a voluntary emigration towards Banja Luka, and that a return to the valley of Japra was definitely impossible, but this population showed no willingness for it." This document, and this sentence, you are quoting, is understood by me and I'll check with my colleagues whether they have the same understanding of this language, that is to say that they could not stay, they could not return to the valley, that what this report said, the remaining possibility, was to expedite a voluntary emigration so that means the only possibility was that they had to leave. But they did not want to do that. That's what my understanding of this language is. So there seems to be a basic difference in understanding of this language, where you invoke the same sentence to a totally different end. Therefore, I wanted to confront you with my understanding and the understanding of both my colleagues, and to explain to us what makes you interpret this sentence in such a different way as we do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, if I understood properly, I don't think that this was translated properly. I was talking with the deputies of the SDA party in the municipal assembly building, and based on their information about the situation in the Japra valley, meaning I didn't actually go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. What you told us, that this last line confirms -- let me just take it very literally so that there is no misunderstanding. You said that you met with some of the deputies from the SDA party who asked you whether they could leave that area. And you said that's what you can see in this line. As a matter of fact, I do not see any request for leaving the area here. What I see on this line is that this report establishes an impossibility to return, sees as the remaining possibility an expedited emigration, and that the population did not want that. So, therefore, this line, as far as we understand it, does not in any way support your testimony as you claimed that the population, as it was explained to you by the SDA representatives, that the population wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My statement, and my assertion is based precisely on the fact that when I was negotiating for the second time with the representatives from the Japra valley and based on what they were asking for and based on their report, when they told me about the situation in the Japra valley I'm just saying just what happened. This sentence, I even think that even grammatically it's not well formulated and it probably causes confusion in the translation, probably in the translation itself, would lead to some sort of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever there is any translation problem we are going to check that so we'll ask to have this specific line read out slowly so that we can check whether the interpretation is right or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to request exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I take up this baton as far as this issue is concerned, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I ask you, very slowly, please, Mr. Pasic, to read out the sentence in question? It begins in the English translation, "The remaining possibility was to expedite." The whole sentence slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Only possibility remained was to conduct a voluntary removal to the -- in the direction of Banja Luka and that the return to the Japra valley was definitely impossible but that population did not show any willingness to do that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The translation we received is where emigration is now translated as removal, is certainly not any less strong than the translation we received on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, ask this supplementary question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you understand that sentence to mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am indeed.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat my statement that I am making now. I am trying to remember the actions and events that happened in that period so that I could understand this sentence more easily. As I said, there were negotiations by the SDA deputies, who were asking me to find a solution so that those people can temporarily move out or go somewhere and to enable them to leave safely that area because it was impossible, and they were asking me if we could guarantee them complete safety, could we protect their houses, their property, could we guarantee their lives, the safety of their lives? As I said, this was practically impossible to do because you would need so many men in order to protect each house in that area, and I could not do that. I could not provide any safety guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there again. You're explaining what, as you testified over the last ten minutes, what the situation was. You claimed that this report would support your view. I confronted you with how the judges read this portion of the report, and then Mr. Josse invited you to tell us exactly what you understood by this one line, what you actually did is that you repeated your view on the situation. You did not tell us how you understand these three lines on from the remaining possibility was. Please tell us how you interpret this. Mr. Josse, I take it that's what you asked the witness, how he understand this is language and not to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, in particular -- yes, perhaps the witness could try again how he understands the language the whole sentence is concerned and then if need be I'll break it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You interrupted me, actually. I wanted to explain. It's hard to do it in two words, to discuss a situation which evolved over a period of days and to explain the sentence that was stated. I repeat, the people who were representing the SDA party and the Muslims, the Bosniaks, in that period, did not want to go in the direction of Banja Luka to the Federation, explaining that they would be mobilised there, that they did not want to be in the uniform of the then Bosnia which was under the leadership of Alija Izetbegovic, but they did ask to leave in a different direction and you will see that in one of the following passages where they sought to go in the direction of Croatia. This is what I think is the sense of this sentence, what that referred to, where they simply did not wish to go in that direction and we told them at the time we can only help you at this time if you want to leave, that you can only leave in the direction of Banja Luka, the direction of Doboj, and then in that area where the line of separation was between Doboj and Maglaj. You can go to that area. I repeat, I think that that is the sense of this sentence because at the time they were refusing to go in that direction but they did request to go in the direction of the Republic of Croatia, and that's how this conversation proceeded. What it is that they wanted our help in, that they wanted us in a way to assure that they could go freely where they wanted to go, to the destination they wanted to go. And the reason they wanted to go in the direction of Croatia was that people in the Japra valley had relatives who were working in -- abroad in Germany, Austria, so their motive was in that way to try to overcome this difficult time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now do I understand that you say you read this line that where the population showed no willingness for it, then that is limited to the direction in which they were to be emigrated or removed. Now, another portion of this line says that the return -- a return to the valley of Japra was definitely impossible. Do I have to understand this, that under the situation existing at that time, it was no option -- you did not consider it possible for the population to return to the valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was that option, and that was the first option for the people to return to their homes, before any of the conversations we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. The line reads, "That a return to the valley of Japra was definitely impossible." Please explain to me what that means in your view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just trying to say what it was that was happening in that period. This report was written about a month later, so chronologically this had already happened. So somebody was interpreting what had already happened in the simplest and easiest possible way. So what I want to say is when those people came to my office, I proposed to them, is there any way to have the following solution that you return to your homes, that you return from Blagaj to your homes? And they explained to me at the time that simply there was fear, insecurity, and they wanted me to provide absolute security guarantees that certain paramilitary formation groups would not appear there, that they would not come to that area, then they would probably go back. Of course, I myself from my aspect, from my competencies as president of the municipal assembly, did not have the power or the competencies to extend these guarantees to them and I was giving this example that -- to them that even while we were sitting here in the office, something unpleasant might happen up there at your houses. I gave them the examples that I really couldn't provide these guarantees for them. It was too great a responsibility for me to guarantee something that I was not responsible for. And for those reasons, when they understood what my competencies were and once I understood them, they suggested to me that they could go in the direction of Croatia. And, if I recall correctly, I think at the time, the only possibility was for them to go in the direction of Banja Luka and Doboj. There was another option which did not suit them at all, and that was the option and perhaps it would have been the simplest option, for them to go from that area and that was to go towards the direction of Bosanska Krupa, which they did not accept at all because they believed that as soon as they left towards Bosanska Krupa, the so-called Cazinska Krajina that they would automatically be mobilised there and that they would be facing the lines towards Serb territory. So what was being talked about here at that time was just the possibility, if they remain, how safe would they be, and whether the Crisis Staff or the TO staff or the public security station could provide them absolute guarantees for security and if they could not, then they asked them -- they asked for us to try to help them to alleviate their problems and to go, let's say n one of these directions. So their wish was to go in the direction of Croatia. We are actually talking about the direction of how they would go and where they would go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One final question: Why didn't you ask the military to go in and get rid of those who were -- who had been looting and why didn't you -- or did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just saying that I was seeking, and I was constantly seeking, we, I, I repeat, every day I went to work, and I sat there and I asked the TO Staff every day and public security station every day to make the ultimate effort to really prevent these paramilitary formations. This was not a request made once. It was a request made a thousand times, at any point, in any situation that's what I was asking. But I repeat I did not have the responsibility. It was not in my jurisdiction, in a way, to be able to prevent these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there any documentation on any decision taken that you ordered someone to go there and to drive out the -- what I understand were just people who committed crimes and -- did you -- is there anything, any order, any document, which can illustrate your, as you said, you are efforts, your repeated efforts, to stop this -- what is described as a rather terrific situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it states here that the conclusions and decisions of the Crisis Staff were accepted. There were several of those types of conclusions, proposals, decisions, by the Crisis Staff where certain suggestions and instructions were given, even it says some kind of order existed. It says here, although in the practical sense of the word we did not have the authority for orders but I'm sure that there was one. I don't have it. If somebody here has it, it would be good for to us look at it but I cannot specifically remember. But I repeat it was not my order, and I'm repeating in these Crisis Staff meetings, it was a working, operational meeting, where there were suggestions, let's say, to the chiefs of the public security station or the commander of the TO staff, let's see what we can do, can we stop this group which was destroying property and doing something else? So giving such suggestions, proposals, I don't know if there were anything like that in written form. There were certain minutes of those sessions. I don't have these unfortunately with me because it was a wartime situation which was going on and I know that a part of the -- these documents were destroyed but I don't know which part was destroyed, if there is anything of that, any notes, it would be good, then I could refresh my recollection. I know that we did take minutes of the meetings and then based on the minutes, once we saw them, you could see that there were such instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also say, we had no competence to issue orders in this respect. It was, let me just find your words. You say in the practical sense of the word, "we did not have the authority for orders." Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the 11th of May, the Crisis Staff, at least that's what I read in this report, issued an order to establish a cease-fire, which at least suggests that the Crisis Staff itself considered itself competent to issue these kinds of orders whereas later on that same page where it describes the events -- bodies were instructed and fully authorised to undermine the work and activity of the aforementioned illegal individuals, at the same session, in a conclusion, the TO municipal staff was instructed to have its units of the military police -- so the language of this report gives limited support to your answer that you had no competence to issue orders in these circumstances. Could you explain why the report repeatedly states that orders were given whereas you now testified that you're not competent, it was -- it was beyond your -- beyond your authority to give orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even though the question is quite long, I think that I did understand it. If really this report on the work of the Crisis Staff -- well, you cannot take it segment by segment. If you take it as a whole, then it's an entire text and according to my views it can only be looked at like that. I think that the word "order" here does not reflect the true meaning actually in the way that it is cited here. I repeat, it was more -- I'm going to say from sort of media reasons, written in this way in order to form the impression -- actually not to spread defeatism, not to spread fear. We had to, in a way, explain that we even perhaps did have some force as a Crisis Staff but in the real sense, in the formal sense, it really did not have the power or did not have any basis, I'm talking about the Crisis Staff now, to be able to issue any orders. We were able to issue orders but we were not competent for orders whereby somebody could do something or not do something. I mean, we could say, yes, issue an order, but the person that the order was being issued to could say, sir, you're not competent and you don't have any right to issue such an order to me. We tried only to act on the basis of our authority. So probably there were such written documents which were written in the form of an order, but there was no legal force behind them, as an order. So this is probably -- I mean I probably understand you when you are saying when we are talking about the word "order," the word "order" itself can be taken to mean that somebody had certain competences but I'm saying actually how things were actually at the time and what we did and how we actually operated. We did not have that legal formulation. I think that word was not used properly and I'm just saying actually for the reasons that I explained that we formed this sort of picture where we were actually acting on the basis of our authority. But in that sense, order, because I mentioned that the public security station was not subordinated to the president of the municipal assembly, that the TO staff was not subordinated to the president of the municipality assembly, Novi Grad, well, it happened in all the municipalities. This was a law. It was exactly known whom they were subordinated to, who could issue orders to them, commands, and certain requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although your answer was quite long, I think I understand it. Please proceed. Yes, Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to understand two things. First of all, what type of report, not a written report, of course, but what was a rapport that you had with the people who were in charge with the TO municipal Defence people? There must have been a commander of that municipal TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you able to meet him in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on a daily basis almost. Not every single day but yes, we did meet because we had offices next to each other, or close to each other, and we did meet. And as it says here, he was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what did he understand? What was his understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in this report, an attempt was made to describe this, if I understood the question correctly, how he viewed the situation. Of course, he too appealed and asked for assistance. He was impotent too and he found it difficult to accept from the moral standpoint and from the standpoint his own remit, competence and authority, and I saw during those discussions that he was worried and concerned for not being able to control the situation, that he didn't have the force and power to control it. And quite literally, as it has been described, some things escaped control, something was happening in one place and then in another place and a third place. So it kept moving and he kept having to keep abreast of some events that were happening but they were happening all over, and as soon as one problem would be solved, another one would crop up. So if I've understood your question, this was troubling and -- to him, and a cause for concern. We is we discussed this every time. We viewed the situation to see what we could do from our positions and how far we were able to influence the situation. So we viewed it from the moral and humane aspect, too. Can we do anything objectively speaking, on the basis of the competence and authority we had? And could we act as human beings as well to do something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, this TO commander, how many men did he have in his group? What was the size, what was the strength, of the police? I mean, I already asked you a question similar to this one but was there a thousand people that he was in charge of or a hundred people? I mean, how many men were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really not an officer. I just did my military service in the former JNA. In formation terms, establishment terms, I wouldn't hazard a guess. But I don't think he had a lot of men at his disposal, on the basis of the information that I received, at least not enough, not a sufficient number of men, to be in full control of the situation. There was the command of the TO staff, there was the chief of TO staff, and he had some assistants in the department, in the TO staff, but how many men he had at his disposal at any given point of time, of the mobilised soldiers, I really can't say. I don't remember. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question: Was the army deployed in that area where you were yourself? The army itself, not talking about the TO, but was the army deployed in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What army are you referring to? What do you mean when you say army and what period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about the month of June, if I'm not mistaken. So at that time, in June, was there an army deployed? Were there any regular troops that were already engaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I remember, I think that all over Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, the former JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, from mid-May, had withdrawn. So if that's what you mean by army, it wasn't on that territory. It wasn't in the area. Not that kind of army. After -- well, whether there is an agreement or international agreement or whatever, that the present Serbia and the then Republic of Yugoslavia or the former SFRY should withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the former socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was, so as a regular army, it didn't exist any more in those areas. So that was its initial form, original form. And the TO Staffs in fact were just -- just their commanding officers were professionals, whereas the soldiers had been mobilised so they weren't actually professional soldiers, the ones who had been mobilised. Just the commanding cadres worked professionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's precisely the point. These men, they were mobilised men. According to you, did they also engage in murders, in burning houses, et cetera, et cetera, that because you were talking about paramilitary formations. I think that that term is confusing somewhat. We don't quite know what we are talking about, and it's all quite unclear. Are you telling us that among those people who were killing men and who were destroying property, were those men who were engaged in the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous interpretation continues] ... got to say that and explain it in a word but I'll do my best. When we mention paramilitary formations, I think I talked about that earlier on, those paramilitary formations appeared from different sources. They appeared -- they were part of the mobilised army who was in Croatia, on the battle front there. They would come on furlough, and they would create these groups of men wearing uniforms and even army rifles, they would come in from the battlefields of Croatia and create problems. And if you read the report carefully, then you can see from a portion of it that even part of these men who had been mobilised and who were under the command of the TO Staff of Novi Grad, you can see that in fact they refused the TO command, and I think that that was referred to as some sort of regional staffs or headquarters. I think that that's how the TO staff was organised. It had regional, small points. And it says here that at one of those regional staff headquarters, they had refused to take -- the command of the TO, and that this person or unit created problems to the legal authorities, as a renegade, in fact. I think that you can see that somewhere, if you read the report carefully, and it relates to the regional staff, if I remember correctly. Some of the villages, they were referred to and they were Agici, Krslje, Krupska, those were the names of the villages, and I think that's the name of the regional staff that created those problems, in fact, and who, quite literally, did not execute the commands of the TO staff. Let me say that certain measures were taken, but you couldn't take any automatic measures, at least that's the information that was fed back to the TO, and some of the perpetrators were punished as well, as far as I know. But I don't remember all the possible ramifications and details of the various incidents, because later on, a military court was set up as well, so they -- steps were taken along the military line, so I don't know that part of the executive power and authority at the level of the republic. I'm really not well-versed in that and whether proceedings were taken or how far they got to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry to insist so much on this point, but do you agree with me that men that were recruited from your municipality, men who had answered to the call, were those same men who all of a sudden became renegades and became perpetrators of various illegal acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood your question correctly, then it's not possible to answer it that way. They were not the renegades, people who were under the control of the TO Staff. It was just a small group of men that did separate and didn't listen to orders coming from the TO Staff, but looking at it globally, in its entirety and in percentages, then a large percentage of men was under the TO command and did follow orders coming from the TO staff and the commander of the TO staff. But also, it also says here that in addition to those paramilitary formation that were on the side, what happened was that even a portion, so not all the regional staff, but a portion, a small group, of men from the regional staff quite literally refused to follow orders issued by the TO commander. If I've understood your question and if I've answered what you wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Thank you. You've understood my question. I'm just going back to this report where we see on page 5 that [English] "TO municipal staff noted that he's unable to have control over the entire municipal territory, as certain groups are distancing themselves from the chain of command, are not obeying orders, and are acting on their own initiative." [Interpretation] Do you see that sentence, sir? Of course, in English on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it's page 2 in the B/C/S. I think so because I have another passage marked which enables me to work it out. Towards bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find that passage but I haven't managed to do so yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 in English, the Crisis Staff session [French spoken], [English] Situation and said that TO staff did not issue to order -- fire on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, my fault entirely. It's page 3. It's page 3 towards the bottom of the page. I am sorry. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just tell me, could you give me the beginning of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [In English] "He noted that he's unable to have control over the entire municipal territory, as certain groups are distancing themselves from the chain of command, are not obeying orders and are acting on their own initiative."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the witness is probably looking at the right place. It's the paragraph that begins, "At the Crisis Staff session held the 12th of May 1992." It's in that paragraph, the passage that the learned judge is quoting from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes, I found it now. Well, an attempt has been made here to describe the situation that I myself have been describing in my own words. I described what I experienced and what happened, and what I was informed about, and the commander of the TO staff is saying in this paragraph that he is facing the kind of problems that I've been describing, if I understand your question. And I have been talking about that problem, and saying that the TO commander was faced with very serious problems without having the power or men to control it all and to put a stop to these events that were taking place. So I think we can say that that becomes apparent on the basis of this portion of the text. And quite simply, you can just interpret this in that slightly different way but the sense of it is the same. The sense of the sentence goes along the lines of what I myself said; of course, using different words. It's just a matter of the text and wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, I think we are far beyond our usual time. So we'll have a break. At the same time, I'd like to ask special attention of the parties, not specifically you, Mr. Josse, but to be very careful with the translation of this document. I just, for example, note that on page 4 of the English translation, there is a list of six points whereas on page 3 of the B/C/S version, we have that same list but now consisting of seven points. The third one not being translated. So that reduces seven to six. So therefore, if there is any doubt as to this document, we should always very carefully check the translation and whether it's complete and whether it's in every respect accurate. Of course, that's what an unrevised translation brings as a risk. We will adjourn until 20 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour can I make this observation? So far as the questions that Your Honour has asked there were a number of passages I was going to take the witness to. I'm sure the Court will look at this unrevised translation as closely as it can but some of Your Honour's questions are answered to a limited extent in this document and it may be if the Court looks at it again, I can deal with it much more speedily after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps -- yes. There is a fair chance that you're more efficient than we sometimes are. We will have a break until 20 minutes past 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. You may proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to deal briefly, I hope, with two passages of this document, which, to some extent, as I've already said, answer the questions posed by His Honour Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At page 5 in the English, bottom of page 3 in the original, there is some discussion in the document, is there not, Mr. Pasic, about instructions, the word used in the translation, given by the Crisis Staff to the Territorial Defence? I'll read a bit of it. "At the same session, in a conclusion, the TO, Territorial Defence Municipal Staff, was instructed to have its units of the military police, with the assistance of the public security station police and, if necessary, the military police from the Banja Luka Corps estimate the situation and take concrete measures of searching the terrain in parts of town with instant occurrence." And then it names the various villages, other settlements in the Japra valley, enforce public law and order and make provisions for the return of the civilian population from the area. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be on the top of page 4 in the B/C/S, which is more likely?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 4 at the top, Mr. Pasic, I think would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I might be allowed a few moments to read through it just briefly, please, because I haven't found the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found it by now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think all my question is, is it confirms, does it not, that an instruction was given to the TO to do something?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In a series of the instructions, proposals, and so on and so forth, we can see from this that we asked that regardless of their presentation, and this referred to the TO staff and public security station, that they should continue to invest every effort to ensure that all these little groups and the excessive behaviour that was taking place, to try and place them under their control, to control the situation, and I think that that's what this passage refers to as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You will remember that we looked in some detail at -- in the B/C/S, the bottom of page 5, I think the last three or four words, so turning on to page 6, about the looting, this is page 9 in the English, but we didn't look at the last part of that paragraph, so I think this is page 6 in your version. Have you got that passage? Page 6 towards the top of the page. I'll read this bit out. It's after it describes the looting. "As the area was a location of many valuable structures, the Crisis Staff had issued" - I assume it's "an order" - "to the regional staff of Donji" -- and then there is an illegible word. I don't know if you can help us with the name of the place that's mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on page 6, or at least I haven't found it there. On my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could assist you, I think it's page 6, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It mentions a mill, a telephone exchange. It is page 6, Mr. Pasic. We are fairly sure about that here. Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 6 starts with the first sentence on page 5 and it said "the order wasn't acted upon and chaos ensued." Is that the passage? And all the places have been totally looted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until -- well, let's say two-thirds of that paragraph, then you find the passage that was just quoted. The part quoted, it's actually the 10th line, the 10th line of page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why don't you read it out in the B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The TO staff expressed" - I think it says expressed, although it's rather illegible. Is this "inability" or is it "assistance"? I can't quite read it -- "in ending this action." That the TO expressed impotence or inability to end the situation like that, but as I say, it's not a very good copy. But I think that's what it says, and that that's the meaning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the next line -- it's the next sentence, Mr. Pasic, where there is also one portion declared illegible. So there is -- where it says, as the area was a location of many --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, valuable structures. I don't know how you're going to interpret this but led me read the sentence out. "As the area was a location of many valuable structures, the Crisis Staff had issued to" - I think it says Donji Agici is the village, "issued an order to Donji Agici to secure some of them so that -- or some of them, yes, "some" is the word, some of them, and then it says the mill, the telephone exchange, the private carpentry shop, et cetera, with Territorial Defence members of the same RS, Regional Staff, I think that is, and the commander of which was designated as personally responsible for carrying out the order, and then there is a full stop there and it goes on to say the order was not carried out because a lot of the equipment, and then in brackets it says, I think this is machinery, electrical motors, et cetera, was looted from the facilities or structures. So it says here who we issued orders to based on the discussions or we discussed the orders, and we even tried to issue orders to that regional staff. That was under the control of the TO Staff, to issue concrete instructions how to stop the looting of property, and this just chooses some of them, quotes some examples, there were probably a lot of facilities like that which they tried to safeguard but were not able to do so because that property was ultimately destroyed. But anyway we did want, as I said a moment ago, to try and become more serious. This was all going into the media, and we wanted prevail upon the ordinary man in the street to show him that the Crisis Staff did have some sort of authority or power or whatever you like to call it, and all this was geared towards one end, that is to say to prevent these groups, little groups, or paramilitary formations, to instill fear in them, to have them realise that they would be punished and that the Crisis Staff would be effective in its measures. So those were the proposals we sent down the line as we did here, and you can see the sense and purpose of the proposal given by the Crisis Staff to try and preserve the property. I don't know if I've explained this fully enough but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
