utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I take it that this is an answer to the question because you only asked to say what Donji and then illegible was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is an answer to where eventually I was going it take the witness. So I'm going to move on to my next point. I don't know whether the Court has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to ask for two or three clarifications. Could you tell us, the mill that's mentioned, was that private property or was that public property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be certain but as far as I know, there was no publicly owned mill in that valley. It was a mill owned by a person who was a Muslim, a Bosniak. If I can remember correctly, I think that at some of the meetings, the joint consultations that we had, it was proposed that some key facilities should be secured, protected, as valuable, because it was simply not possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you answered my question. I'm quite satisfied. You say as far as you remember it was privately owned and it was owned by a Muslim. Private carpentry shop, do you remember who owned that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was also private property. In that area -- well, you have the map in front of you, I hope, and you saw that area. That area was mostly inhabited by Muslims and I think that that carpentry shop was also owned by a Muslim. It was privately owned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say that is what you think. You're not sure about it but that's what you -- on the basis of the population what you expect? Or do you have any more specific knowledge about ownership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that area that we are talking about, then and now, there were no publicly owned companies or state-owned companies, and based on that, I conclude that this was private property and that the owner -- because I remember in the village of Supaca [phoen], there was a larger carpentry shop where a Muslim Bosniak was the owner and I think that refers to that because from Blagaj to Gornji Agici, those villages up there, there were no state-owned firms where that could be interpreted differently, that the property was of any other kind other than property -- personal property, and there was no other large carpentry shop except for this one in the place of Suhaca and that shop was owned by a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse. And may I ask you, Mr. Pasic, sometimes you give a lot of detailed information where sometimes the one who asked the question might not need all those details, which, of course, take time. If further details are needed, you'll certainly be asked for it, but try to keep the answers brief to the extent possible and reasonable. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we move to tab 2, please, D15, which we looked at a little bit earlier. This, as is clear from the document, is a decision in June of 1992. What do you read the date as, Mr. Pasic? Because the translation is a little unclear as to the exact date. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we are talking about the same thing here, we have the conclusions of the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly at its meeting which was held on the 16th of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you just -- your attention is drawn to the top, where, second line, there could be some question as to the exact date. How do you read that? Where it says "datum."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the date, if we look in the upper hand corner, underneath the decision, and the conclusion, it says the 18th of June 1992, but if you look at the preamble of the conclusion, then there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's, I think, what Mr. Josse asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just as simple as whether it's the 18th and he didn't specify that, whether it's the 13th or 18th, which is logical. I don't think it needs further attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Moving to the conclusion we have to some extent earlier examined number 1 and it speaks for itself. Number 2, again, I'm going to leave at least for a moment because 3 and 4, to some extent, again arise from some of the questions asked by the learned Judges. We see, so far as number 3 is concerned, Judge Hanoteau specifically asked about this. It urges that all necessary steps be taken to form a brigade similar to a battalion of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it? That's what it says?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why was it thought urgent, and indeed necessary, for such a battalion to be established?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because of all the things that I stated, the manner of activity, the jurisdiction and the competence of the TO which proved itself to be inefficient in that form of organisation and that type of army. All of that is talked about in tab 1 here in the report on the work, and, of course, we were not satisfied with that manner of work, i.e. the functioning of the TO Staff, and it was considered that that TO Staff was not connected to any other activities and actions and it didn't have the power and the authority to stop these events that I was talking about. Our opinions, the opinions of the municipal assembly, which adopted this conclusion, was that it was essential and it was urgent to stop all of these unfortunate events and that a real, proper formation, as it states here, a formation, a brigade formation of a battalion type, to transform this TO Staff into the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that point in time, that was the prevailing opinion, that based on everything that we had seen and analysed, this chaotic situation, the general conclusion was that that type of functioning of the TO, of course, normally was not efficient and it did not carry out what was being asked of it to establish law and order, together with the forces of the police, and for those reasons it was asked that the authorised institutions and organs act in order to organise this battalion as fast as possible, which in our opinion should have been more effective, more disciplined, in order to prevent these little groups of paramilitary formations to stop repeating themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as item number 4 is concerned, and you were asked by Judge Orie as to whether there had been any order in relation to security, this instructs the public security station and the military police command to establish public law and order and the security of its inhabitants in Bosanski Novi. Now, you've already given us a fair amount of explanation as to why this was necessary. In relation to this specific conclusion, is there anything you can add?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said what the competencies were of the TO staff at the time and that's why this item 3 and 4 in a way is sort of separate. They are kind of separate entities and what was thought that for these things to be improved in the military sense and as I mentioned I don't want to repeat again, this formation about the battalion, the public security station was asked thus together with the commands of the military police. I think this proposal was given to set up or establish public law and order because that was their task, for them specifically to maintain law and order. The police were supposed to do this. I repeat, thus -- well, let's not repeat ourselves then. When we are formulating this part, is being asked -- is being requested to -- these were forms of suggestions, appeals, if I may translate that freely, like this, but this was a way to make it known that both sides, the military and the civilian police forces, were being asked for a more effective and faster action in order to establish discipline and to prevent all of these unfortunate events which were happening in that past period. So this was confirmed again at this meeting of the municipal assembly, which was adopted, as it says here, on the 16th of June, as it says up here, the actual document was drafted on the 18th and this is where the dilemma comes from about which date is correct. The meeting was on the 16th and the text was drafted on the 18th. I don't know whether that is your regular practice but this is how we used to do it when something was adopted and then when something was actually drafted in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to item 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Item 2 of this same document, I leave you with the document and wait with any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour if I could suggest additional questions might be an idea now because I'm going to use number 2 to lead on to the problems with these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just explained to us that decisions were taken and then put on paper. I asked earlier about orders in relation to the events in the Japra valley. Are there any such written orders and instructions in relation to the -- establishing public law and order from that time? Because from what I understand, comparing the report on the Crisis Staff activities with this document, that that matter had been settled already by the 16th or the 18th of June, where the people were allowed to move out on the 8th of June, as the other document says. So I'm asking whether there were any similar orders from the time of the events in the Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the documents here. Probably there is a paper trail, but at this point in time, I really cannot recall it, but I repeat, at the meeting of the -- meetings of the Crisis Staff, minutes were taken and some of those conclusions were formulated, whether as formulations of proposals or so on, but there were things like that, but at this point in time, I really cannot remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then one tiny little thing. At the top of this document, in our translation, some words are reported as being illegible. If I read the two very top lines, is it true that the first one starts with Srpska Republika? Is that how you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the second line, does that start with the word "Skupstina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's council -- that's assembly? Skupstina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the translation could be the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the municipal assembly of Bosanski Novi. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I first leave you with number 2, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, number 2 is a repetition of something that's in the Crisis Staff report. I haven't checked whether it's word for word but it deals with the Muslims of the municipality, and it says that the Muslims may leave voluntarily in an organised and civilised manner, that any activities directed at forceful expulsion is banned, and then it goes on to deal with the reception centre of the Mlavke stadium. Now, by this time, you had already begun your negotiations with the international community in relation to these Bosniak people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it might be a convenient and easier way of dealing with this. To begin with, if we look at tab 3, and look at the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could be given one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which I think is P125. It says P126, on it, Your Honour, I think that's a mistake. Perhaps the Court will check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's a mistake because at the copy in the hands of the Registry -- no. It might be -- I've got 126. The problem is that these -- no, no. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, from my records, this appears to be a part of P126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just wondering whether it's -- yes. The faxed transmission is a part of 126. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. The difficulty we had in preparing these documents is in the official court exhibit list, 125 and 126 are described in almost identical fashion and therefore -- perhaps had we gone back to the transcript we might have been able to sort it out but on the face of the exhibit list, it was impossible to stand them apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got the list with me at this moment but at least the cover page of 125 bears as the date the 26th of May 1992, whereas 126 cover page, the first page of that exhibit, is 1st of June 1992. But very similar forms. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to find the B/C/S translation of this original English document, and you should find it somewhere in tab 3. It bears at the top right-hand corner the number 03066808. And this is a note or report prepared by Jens Brostad of a meeting he held with you on the 28th of May of 1992. You are mentioned in paragraph number 2. He sets the scene in paragraph number 1 of what the position was. I'm going to ask you one or two selective questions about the document and then perhaps you could tell us about your recollection of this meeting. But perhaps before I do that, at this point, had you met Mr. Kirudja? In other words, on the 28th of May 1992, where you had a meeting with Mr. Brostad, had you met Mr. Kirudja on any previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is contemplating his answer, I believe, in the course of the testimony, that the date of the 28th of May 1992, which is found at the top of this report, was corrected in court to be the 27th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not in my recollection at the moment. That's -- thank you, Mr. Harmon, for -- but was it only on the top or also in paragraph 2 where --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I recall Mr. Kirudja testifying that the meeting that was recounted in this document was held on the 27th of May and I think he corrected this document as part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the 28th appears twice, not only in the -- yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So in other words, was this the first time you met Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Kirudja but I don't remember whether it was the 27th or the 28th or some other date. It was at Topusko which is in today's Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And again, it might help to put this into some sort of context if I ask you how many meetings did you have in total with Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to say exactly how many, but I know that these talks went from Dvor Na Uni and Topusko which is in Croatia, now we also had talks at the UNPROFOR base at Dvor. We also had talks at the bridge which divides Bosnia and Croatia. It's a bridge on the river Una. But I really cannot give you an exact number, whether it was two, three, or five, I don't know. There were more than two but I really wouldn't be able to say exactly how many. I simply don't remember. I know that there were several of those kinds of conversations, not only with Mr. Kirudja but with other representatives from this committee for refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, were you asked about meetings with Mr. Kirudja. If Mr. Josse would like to know whether you met other people he will certainly ask you. We are under some time constraints. So let's proceed. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Particularly bearing in mind that answer we will try as best we can to work from these documents although I hope that that won't turn out to be more rather than less time consuming. The document I'm about to ask you about, paragraph 6, it says the situation, and it says, Mr. Rade, who did most of the talking for the visitors. Who was Mr. Rade? Sorry. Yes. This doesn't help at all. It's in fact paragraph 4 in translation, it says 4 in translation. In English it says 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. English counting always has been a bit surprising for all of us, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got no retort to that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it here. It's item 4 in my language. It says, "The situation" if we are thinking of the same thing, Rade Palije, first name Rade, last name Palije. I cannot be specific but I think his function in these talks were because he knew English and French very well and he was the one who went with me to make the initial contacts. He was there at hand so that we could communicate more easily, if I can put it that way, although he was perhaps even a member of the executive board, but as a volunteer, not in a professional capacity. In a certain period I know that he was a member of the executive board, but these were volunteers for education, culture, sports and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, whether he volunteered or whether -- what your answer could have been as -- by the way, Mr. Josse, we find it in the document itself as well, that Mr. Palije Rade was a member of the executive council, I take it of your municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I was thinking of the Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, whether he was sent by his wife or whether he did it on his own, whether he volunteered, that's if we would like to know that, we'll ask you about it, or Mr. Josse will ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, probably it would have helped if I had led in something like that. All I was trying to establish is that he was basically an interpreter and he spoke good English and French.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This meeting at Topusko, what were you trying to achieve?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just what I was saying earlier, when we were talking about the report of the Crisis Staff, you could see that representatives of the Muslim people asked me for help to find a solution how they could move out of the Novi Grad municipality area. So, based on what they were seeking I was trying to find a solution. We didn't even know how this could be resolved but for the first time we addressed the Dvor municipality and somebody from there said that people in charge of civilian questions were in Topusko. I didn't know who was there. It was an informative meeting, an informative talk, what can be done vis-a-vis this situation, how can we help these people, what were their requests, how can we agree on this, how can we make their problems a little bit easier?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to help us specifically with paragraph number 9, where it is claimed by the author of the report that after much hesitation, two local Bosniaks were named. Do you recall hesitation on your part in naming Bosniak representatives?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I hesitated over anything. I initiated the meeting and I even proposed that Mr. Kirudja, who attended the talks with me, should be convinced of what I was -- said. And I did, and I can say that subjectively. I did gain the opinion that Mr. Kirudja doesn't believe what I was telling him in one way or another. And then I thought that perhaps he didn't understand me and that Mr. Rade and the official interpreter hadn't translated what I had said properly. So I proposed that some of the Muslim representatives should come and talk to him, if possible, and then we said Topusko Dvor Na Uni could be a possible place for this meeting to take place because the mission did not have a mandate for going all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. They told me that. They said that that was not their mandate, and they didn't have competence or UNPROFOR didn't have the authority to cross the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I know there were some problems along those lines. So I said, well, gentlemen, if you like, I'll propose somebody or you can propose somebody so that you don't have my own personal choice but you could discuss the problems with these people and see what they want, what they are asking for. Now, I don't remember that I hesitated in any way. Quite the contrary. It was I who insisted upon a meeting like that taking place, to solve our problems as soon as possible. It was an appeal, if we had accepted the proposal by the Crisis Staff, to see that the problem should be settled as soon as possible and stop all the adverse things that were going on and to bridge the difficulties, and one of those ideas along those lines was to try and solve it with Mr. Kirudja or rather the representatives of that particular institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the light of that answer, could we examine the next-but-one paragraph which I will read in whole. It says, "In discussing the right of the representatives to speak with us directly and participate in informing the situation and in decisions relating to them, CAC, presumably civil affairs coordinator, in other words, Mr. Kirudja, was blunt in saying we should stop pretending the persons were leaving voluntarily. It was admitted by the representatives that if we met with these persons directly, we would hear that they did not want to leave." Two questions. First of all, do you recall Mr. Kirudja being blunt and saying that the persons were leaving voluntarily -- were not -- I beg your pardon, were not leaving voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember some of his words but I don't remember that particular one, or at least as it has been interpreted to me. But there is a word that I seem to recall and is imprint on my mind, I'm not going to perhaps use the exact word but it was along those lines. Mr. Kirudja told me, he said, Mr. Pasic, our mission is to help the refugees, not to exert any forcible expulsion or voluntary expulsion, and I said, well, I'm not asking for that. I'm asking for you to assist the refugees and then I quoted examples of refugees that had left Croatia. They were Serb refugees it would had left Croatia. So I asked for help and assistance to settle the problem of the Serb refugees who had come into Novi Grad and how to settle the problem that we had discussed in the Japra valley and in the Novi Grad municipality. So my question to Mr. Kirudja was this: Can you truly help us? Can you really help us? And if he doubted what I was telling him, what I was saying, that he could feel free to talk to the representatives of the Muslim ethnic group so that he could become convinced and aware of their opinions because they had asked me to mediate and help them. I didn't go of my own free will to Topusko, it was at the initiative of those representatives, the representatives of the ethnic Muslims that I went there to try to solve the problem. Of course, my conscience dictated to me that the problem should be solved as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next question is that last sentence. It says here quite clearly that it was admitted by the representatives, presumably you and Rade, that if the UN officials met with those persons directly, they would hear that they did not want to leave. Did you or Mr. -- well, did you say that in your language? That's really -- you can't obviously say what Mr. Rade may have said in a language you didn't understand, but did you say that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that that was a very rough translation of the sentence. We were very frank. We spoke very openly, and discussed the problem and I tried to explain the motives where Mr. Kirudja asked me why people wanted that. Of course, had there not been a war and had the situation not been what it was, then quite certainly those people would not have left their homes. So they would have probably stayed on in their homes. But the political, economic and security reasons why such that these were motives for them to leave, and for which the people wanted to leave Novi Grad. So you can't look at it unilaterally and say those people didn't want to go or wanted to go because if we do it that way then we won't understand the problem that the area was facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's clear, I think you would accept this, that there were no Bosniak representatives at this particular meeting. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened after this? In your next meeting with Mr. Kirudja, were Bosniak representatives present?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe I'm not going to get the meetings right in chronological order so, please, excuse me if I mix up some meetings but I know that there were meetings, they did take place in the hotel at Dvor Na Uni and at the UNPROFOR base as well in Dvor Na Uni, and that there was a meeting which I would say was essentially -- took place at the bridge itself, halfway on the bridge, above the river Una, between the Dvor Na Uni and Novi Grad municipalities or, rather, in between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, halfway. And one of those meetings, let me repeat, the meeting on the bridge, at that meeting there were representatives of the Muslim ethnic group but I'm not sure whether they attended one or two meetings that were held in the UNPROFOR meeting. I think there were Muslim representatives there too but I can't be quite sure about that because it's been a long time since then. I know about the bridge meeting, that they were there 100 per cent. As to the other meetings, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As you understand it, what happened in relation to your offer that we see detailed in this minute of the meeting of the 28th of May that UNPROFOR representatives meet up with Muslim representatives or families? What exactly happened, as you understand it, in that regard?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the course of the discussion itself, in my opinion, and we can see that now, that the representatives of the mission did not have -- did not trust us, did not have confidence in what we were saying whereas we did our very best to explain the situation to them as objectively as possible and I think the turning point in all this was the fact that the representatives of the Muslims themselves asked and we allowed them to do so and we wanted them to do so, to attend the meetings and to explain their position, and once the people from the mission realised this, that was a turning point. And on one occasion, I don't remember at what particular meeting I said, "Gentlemen, if you really don't believe us, I don't know how to convince you that what we are saying is correct. It's your right to disbelieve us, but then what you should do is to hold independent talks, independent of myself or the Serbs, find four or five Muslim families to talk to them, without our knowledge, if you like. Talk to them and then you'll get the truth from them and they will be able to tell you what they really want." And that was done on one occasion, that is to say I didn't know that a meeting was taking place or which family they were going to talk to or when, but I later received information at some subsequent meetings that we had, whereas I think Jens or Jensen was present and another gentleman. I think his name was Jean-Claude Coquillateur [phoen] or whatever. I'm sorry, I apologise for my pronunciation, but they said that they had actually talked to the Muslim representatives, to their families in their houses, without our presence, without the presence of the police or any army or anything like that. So they conducted these discussions independently and autonomously and they came to realise, as I was told, that what I tried to explain to them was right, and which was the dilemma that they had at all our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were the Serb authorities in any way party to those meetings with the Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said no, they weren't. Nobody attended those meetings with those families. No Serbs. No ethnic Serbs. None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would just like to get your opinion on the following. You were talking to some people. You were talking to your counterparts. Now, wasn't the problem this one? Were they in fact in doubt that these Muslims did not want to leave on their own? Or did they try to understand why did they want to leave voluntarily? You've told us not long ago that there was a chaotic situation in the municipality, but for your counterparts, such as Mr. Kirudja, who was maybe not on the ground, one of the most important things to understand at the time was not to determine what was making these people willing to leave. Yes, of course, they were probably not willing to leave on their own free will but they had to leave because of the things that were happening in their own country, because of the conditions that they were in and who and why was the situation so different and so difficult? This is what they had to establish. Would you agree with me on that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a long question and if I've understood it correctly, you would like my opinion -- well, both then and now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt, sir, but what I would like to know is whether you understand that people such as Mr. Kirudja -- I'm just putting myself in his shoes, I don't know if that was really the problem but do you understand that your counterpart may have said yes, of course, these people are willing to leave, of course, they are willing to leave, but there is a reason for that, and that is that in their own country, in their own state, they did not live in very good conditions. Do you understand or did you understand at the time that there may have been this -- that kind of feeling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean Mr. Kirudja's hesitation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, but also other people from that same organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be quite frank, I really did understand it. Perhaps I would have behaved in the same way had I been in their place, and I wouldn't have taken any hasty decisions. Let me repeat, had I been in their position. I would have investigated. So that's why the discussion went on for such a long time. And I've already said that. I think there was a sort of doubt present in their mind, a lack of confidence and trust in what we were saying. They didn't fully believe us. And I could understand that. I understood Mr. Kirudja's doubts. When you look at it from the aspects of peace this might even appear ironic that somebody wanted to leave their homes of their own free will voluntarily, but as I said, there were a number of motives which these people asked to leave the area they were living in and had been brought up in. It's difficult to explain, of course, and it's difficult to understand for the man in the street, ordinary people, to understand why somebody would want to leave their own home. But as I said, there were a number much reasons why they wanted to do that, when I discussed the report on the Crisis Staff. I tried to explain the reasons for which people did wish to leave and why they in fact did leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just this. In paragraph number 9 we have been looking at in some detail, it mentions two Muslim representatives. Briefly, gentleman named as number 1, is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know how he died?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I received information later that he didn't die a natural death but that he was killed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And number 2?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the same thing happened to the second man, Mr. Hamzagic [phoen]. He was a deputy in the SDA assembly and I later learned that the two of them had been killed, that they didn't die a natural death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us anything about where and by whom they were killed? Or what you heard about that? I take it that you did not personally observe that but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, I did not personally observe that. But I don't remember when that information came my way. But anyway I did learn that they were killed in some of the clashes where those paramilitaries were rampant around the Japra valley and so on, but I can't be exact. The information I received didn't include the exact locality of their deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the Japra valley events you described before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the events in the Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely the period described in the report on the work of the Crisis Staff. That is to say, from the 11th -- 10th, 11th of May onwards, until sometime around mid-June perhaps or a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although isn't it true that the events that is from the report, I remember that mortars were fired, civilian population left the Japra valley and since we are now dealing with larger amounts of refugees that this meeting took place once the Japra valley was already -- that civilians were not living there any more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If this is the 27th or 28th of May, then that would be roughly around the 20th to the 25th perhaps. I can't say exactly. But any way, that part of the population had already been moved from the upper villages to the village of Blagaj and Sifet Bajrautarevic and Fikret Hamzagic, these two people who knew me personally, they were deputies in the municipal assembly, they came to see me with a request that I really do something to help them because they wanted to leave, and that's -- and the problem was whether they wanted to go to Banja Luka or Croatia, which direction. So they asked me that, and I said that a moment ago, that they -- there was this option of going towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you exclude that the two gentlemen had died already by the 27th or the 28th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one other name from the Bosniak community, Izet Muhamedagic, was he still living in Bosanski Novi at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's alive and living in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was his position? He'd been president of the executive committee of the Bosanski Novi SDA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the president of the SDA party in Bosanski Novi. Well, his position was almost identical to the positions I described a moment ago, and Mr. Muhamedagic, I remember -- I don't remember what the date was, whether it was May or the beginning of June, I'm not quite sure there, but anyway, he came -- I think he came to my office and that he asked -- and even tried to explain to us and said that that was the -- a political position taken by the SDA party itself at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they should peacefully, voluntarily be enabled to move out from Bosnia-Herzegovina. He meant the Muslim population. So all that then confirmed or rather came from the representatives of the Muslims themselves and all my attempts were to lessen the troubles and problems that these people were facing, and they gave some ideas as to how those problems could be solved. So I didn't have a special vision myself of how the problem could be solved but we pooled our efforts and tried to solve the problem jointly, to make it as less painful for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And your understanding as far as this gentleman's concerned is that he in fact was a deputy justice minister in Mr. Izetbegovic's government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic [as interpreted], for reasons unbeknownst to me, was not part of the bigger group when the Muslims went and were escorted by UNPROFOR but left Bosanski Novi according to some unofficial channels, I think that a group of Serbs escorted him into the present Republika Srpska Krajina which is Croatia today, and that they traversed the same route these people traversed later on, that he left that same way, and later on, he was assistant minister for legal affairs in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was led by Mr. Izetbegovic and the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It came out in translation as "Mr. Izetbegovic." You were talking about Mr. Muhamedagic. That's right? You just described him, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood the question you asked me about Izet Muhamedagic who was present at the SDA in Novi Grad, is that right? But I might have made a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have made a slip of the tongue and said Izetbegovic but who I meant to say was Izet Muhamedagic who was president of the SDA in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right that he was subsequently killed in a helicopter crash along with some other government ministers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that through the media. I think it was 1993, 1994, in the territory of the present Croatia. At least that's what the television broadcast announced, that he had been killed along with Ljubijankic, who was Minister of Justice, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it would next be useful if we can, please, to look at tab 5, or at least the first two photographs in tab 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, does -- do the photographs need an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They do, Your Honour. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph found at tab 5 will be given Defence Exhibit D116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 116, and then perhaps you give A for the -- no, we have three photographs. Let's number them A, B, C, A being the photograph of the man in camouflage uniform and hand at his nose, second one the photograph on which in the background appears a car, licence plate M 11074. And the third one is a landscape with quite a lot of buses on it. That's C. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, these, as we can see, are black and white photographs. In fact, you have the original colour photographs in your possession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You do not want to relinquish those colour photographs. You want to retain them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very helpfully, you prepared a CD of those colour photographs,?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that we could make an exhibit if in due course anyone wants to see the colour copies. The problem is we don't -- we didn't have the facilities to put the colour -- the CD on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, what do the colours add to what we see in the black and white?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nothing, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's just keep it to the three black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, these -- the first two photographs were clearly both taken at the same time. Briefly tell us who took them.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned, this was taken by a photographer or rather journalist, whether he was from Denmark or Belgium, I'm not quite sure, but he wasn't somebody from those parts, and he attended those negotiations and meetings, and this is a picture taken on the bridge that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the -- this was, as you've just said, the bridge negotiation. The gentleman in the middle with the beard, is that the man you know as Mr. Jens, who I think you can assume is Mr. Brostad?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see on the screen, that's the person who is holding a notepad or some paper in front of him. I received information that that was Jensen [as interpreted], that that man was called Jensen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's how you knew him as Mr. Jensen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can see you as we look at the photograph to the left. Who are the two men that we see in military fatigues?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people in the military uniform next to me and next to Mr. Jensen are both from the Dvor municipality. They were officials in the Dvor Na Uni municipality, that is the then Serb republic -- the Republic of Serbian Krajina and present Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The gentleman to the right, whose wrist watch we see very clearly, I'm not -- from which community did he come?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see here on the left and the right side, representatives of the Muslim people who were negotiating together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea when this photograph was taken? I suppose, again, bad question. Specific idea. We know vaguely when it was taken but are you able to help us with the exact date?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't venture to say, because I don't remember the dates but I think that this is a period sometime after these talks with Mr. Kirudja, so it could be perhaps June, I don't know whether it's early June or late June. We could say that it was more likely that it was late June because, as I mentioned to you earlier, after this meeting, I think that after this meeting, these talks took place with representatives of the Muslim ethnic group independently, without the presence of anybody from the Serb ethnic group. I could be wrong but I think it's probably late June, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could you ask also to identify the representatives of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour that's a matter perhaps I could -- I am going to turn to that, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask you this? We can see in the distance Bosanski Novi, clearly the river underneath. The photograph has been taken from the Croatian side, so to speak. Why was the meeting held on this bridge?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that there was a dilemma about the mission's mandate, the mission of these gentlemen from Topusko. And then I think Mr. Jensen at the time we were speaking said that his mandate didn't permit him to cross into Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said for me it doesn't matter where we meet. It's important to try to resolve something so the place where it would be held didn't really mean anything because even though that day was quite hot and we spent some two or three hours standing on that bridge and it was quite uncomfortable, let's say, in that sense, I mean the physical sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We will turn if we may to the third photograph later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can confirm this, the third photograph the one of the buses was taken on a completely different day, is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll come back to that a little bit later. Related to the evidence that you've just given and an important part of the negotiations was the people who were being housed, putting it neutrally, in the football stadium. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Which people? You mean at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, no. Sorry. An important part of the negotiations concerned the plight and welfare of those individuals who were being housed in the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did refer to them, to them also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see reference to the stadium in tab 2, where the municipal assembly had said in paragraph 2 of tab 2 that those people should be treated humanely. And I might add, in the spirit of regulations on detainees and prisoners. What is your recollection, as to how it was that a significant number of people came to be housed at the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible so as not to take up too much time and I will also try to be concise and clear. So as I say, sometime in late May, what happened was what we already mentioned, that the people came down from the upper villages to Blagaj and that this whole situation was -- happened. We were doing negotiations with Mr. Kirudja and we were trying to find a solution and that representatives of Mr., as I mention him here, Sifet Bajrautarevic and Hamzagic, I think his name was, Fikret, we were trying to find a solution how to help those people. I repeat, I'm perhaps repeating it for the third time, that they did not want to go in the direction of central Bosnia, under the pretext that they would be mobilised there and they simply did not want to carry weapons and fire. They wanted to go to Europe where they would meet their families, those who had families, family members who were already working in Europe. So that was what the conversation was about that I already mentioned. But, as the situation continued to be tense and very difficult, and I really don't remember exactly what day it was, but I assume it was sometime approximately the same in late May or early June, it was probably more likely to be early June, that they agreed to go towards Central Bosnia or in the direction of Banja Luka, rather, towards the line of separation between Doboj and Maglaj. This was done, and I repeat, from the Japra valley, from those villages. Those people were then placed into railway cars and went towards Doboj by rail. That's where we, and when I say we, I mean the municipality people who were doing something at the time, we didn't know that they would return from that -- that the militarily-able people, men, would be returned from Doboj and that there, only the elderly, the women and children were allowed to pass from that column, from that train. That problem simply happened to us. It was created just like a series of other problems were created. That's how this problem also just happened. Having learned from the situation and based on what had previously happened in the Japra valley, and out of fear that something even worse would happen to them, we simply didn't dare return these people to the Japra valley again, those people who had been returned from the column, those people who were going towards Doboj. Then there was a proposal that they should be located somewhere where in some way they -- we would be able to guarantee them some kind of security and safety. At that moment, it was suggested that an adequate solution would be the football stadium in Novi Grad because there are other facilities there at the stadium such as a restaurant some dormitories. There was some catering establishments along the stadium and they could be adapted so these people could temporarily stay there. Then all these talks that had already been started with Mr. Kirudja were giving us hope that this problem which had suddenly cropped up would be resolved quickly and that we could finish that case very quickly. Unfortunately, this was shifted to some months or something, that's what I recall, and precisely that time period of their stay really depended on all of these negotiations that I mentioned with the commissariat or commissioner for refugees from Topusko and the authorities from Dvor Na Uni.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever personally visit the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was responsible for running it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could notice based on what I said before that the TO Staff was responsible, the TO Staff command engaged part of those mobilised soldiers who then were securing and guarding those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was your understanding as to the conditions that the people were being kept in?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those people were definitely not ones that they could have had at their homes but we tried to give them a kind of humane service. We also tried to give them a sense of security so that these incidents which were carried out by paramilitary formations would not happen. I must say that those people were even permitted to receive visits from family members who happened to be in town itself, meaning that some of the Muslim population who were still in town and where there was control in that area, to some extent. These people could visit them and we fed them and as far as I can recall, they were fed from the same place where the soldiers were being fed, and I was informed that they received regular meals, they slept in the premises that I mentioned, and I repeat they were allowed to receive visits from their close relatives and families and, if necessary, these people could even bring them food or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's be clear. It may be worth clarifying your long answer. The people detained there, as far as you were concerned, were all men because their women and children had been allowed to depart at Doboj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it was the men who had been sent back to Bosanski Novi, and it was the men that you had to deal with, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as far as you were aware, no women or children were held there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I'm aware, there were no women or children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The men who were held there had all come from the Japra valley, as far as you were concerned; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, these militarily able men were from the Japra area, the men who were returned from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the Bosniak community of the actual town of Bosanski Novi were concerned, what had happened to them at the time that these men were being held in the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already explained that once but I will repeat. The town itself was easier to keep in control, although there was no real control. Simply these TO staff units and the police tried in a way to maintain public law and order, if we can call it that, and for those reasons, these people stayed in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You would presumably accept, bearing in mind the use of the words in tab 2, "Detainees and prisoners," that these people were not free to come and go?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say it like that because they were there and I repeat the main motive in a way was their security and safety. If we look at things from this aspect now, they did not have all the freedoms, but the restriction of freedom was a result of the overall situation that had been created in the entire territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, your answer says they did not have all the freedoms. Let's be very clear. Were they allowed to leave the stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, the stadium, as far as I can recall, and -- was left -- actually those people who guaranteed that they had relatives in the town itself, who still lived in their own houses, they left the stadium. I don't have the exact information about how many people were released at that point, but according to some estimates and stories I heard later, I think about half of those people were located in the town itself. They didn't go to the Japra valley but they were staying with friends and relatives in town. People even went to Serb homes, those who had Serb friends went there so they were taken care of and in a safe place for the time being, in town, in those houses in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say many of them were allowed if they had family members there. How could I reconcile with this answer with one of your previous answers which was to the extent that they were even allowed to receive visits from the family members? I'm not just trying to imagine the situation which is that I have a family member living in town, I am now taken from my own security to a football stadium where, as you said, conditions were not the same as at home. Now, I'm allowed to go and to my family members but I rather stay there and receive them to visit me? Is that how I have to understand it? Because that's part of your two answers. They were even allowed, you said "even allowed," to receive family visits from the town, and you say they did not enjoy all of the freedoms, but they could go to the family members. Now, I'm just trying to understand how someone chooses to remain in that stadium although he can freely go to his family members in the city, in the town, but instead prefers to have these family members, which are even allowed to visit him, to come and go to the stadium. I'm just putting to you what comes into my mind if I carefully listen to your answers and to assist me in properly understanding your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. It's not about whether somebody wanted to or not or wished to and did not. These problems were created here which needed to be resolved at that given time. I repeat: Because of security reasons, because these people happened to find themselves at the stadium. That's what I was informed of initially, those first few days, first, 2nd, third, fifth day. That's what I was told. How the families came and I don't know how they knew that they could accept these people, put them up, have them stay with them, this is something that didn't happen all at once. It happened over that five-day period. I don't know whether it was on the second day, the fifth day or the tenth day that two, three or 15 people left. It happened that families would come and then it happened that those people would leave with those families but I repeat, this would only happen in the area of the town itself, where there was some kind of a safety zone, where law and order was maintained in the town area. They didn't say that they didn't want to leave the stadium but there was a solution found in the sense that, was it a good solution for that person to go and stay with that -- their family, their relatives, and so that it wouldn't happen that perhaps the person and the relatives would be harmed as well. It wasn't all done at the same time. I repeat, the people who were responsible there, the TO staff command, made a kind of assessment at the time and at a given point in time, they would release those people, let them leave the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse. I have to look at the clock as well because we are close -- yes -- one question from Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very short question. This morning, you told us that the TO was completely disorganised. You told us that the commander of the TO was not in a position to control some of his men. You tell us that the stadium was under the control of the TO. Weren't you supposed logically to worry about what could happen at the stadium because the stadium was placed under the orders of an organisation that was completely disorganised and how do you explain the following, as a representative of the municipality, as the head of the Crisis Staff, how come you did not take the necessary precaution, how come you didn't visit that was called -- a place that was called a place of protection? Or that was meant to provide protection to these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A situation was created where we had no choice. Of course, it was not the proper solution. It was probably not the right choice. But we didn't have a different solution or a different option other than the army that we had at the time, the ones that you described in the way that you did just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer my question. You said this morning that it was sheer and utter chaos, that the commander of the TO was not able to control some of these men, some of his men, any more. We have a housing centre, protection centre, being organised in your own municipality. Why, as a citizen, as an official of the municipality, as an official of the Crisis Staff, why didn't you -- didn't you have the idea to go and see what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really would not be able to give you an answer but it's true that I did not go to visit the stadium. I think that I was preoccupied with a different kind of problem. I thought in a way that that was the job of the TO Staff. That it was more of a military question in a way, that it was a question for the police. My tasks were directed at these talks that I spoke about, so I was more focused on that. In a way we were dividing the problems that were being created right in front of us, that were occurring. So my job as the president of the municipality, if I may say, was to try to find a solution of how to solve that problem, and what we looked at now were these meetings that related to that. That's one of the reasons. The other reason is that if you looked at the map, that stadium is on the way out, in the direction of Bosanska Krupa. I lived on the other side of town, and I simply didn't even pass by there, by the stadium at that time, because I don't know at this point, I don't even know if I had time then to visit the stadium and to see the actual state of affairs. So everything that I'm saying I'm saying based on information and reports which I received from the TO Staff command at those meetings, at those sessions, about these things that related to the stadium. I repeat: I was more focused on the talks with people from UNPROFOR and the people from the commission for refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to finish, Mr. Josse. Is there anything? If there would be one or two remaining questions, of course you can put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's -- can I just see how I get on, Your Honour? Because in relation to what's just been asked, I think it's worth looking at tab 1 again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Page 9 at the bottom in English. Page 6 in the middle, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It says, "For security reasons the military police had concentrated a large number of civilians of military age at the Mlavke stadium. They were to be held until the weapons' sweep was completed and then interrogated. As the persons were held for a long time, four days, they incurred high costs for the holding period in security, food and lodging, and a counter-effect was created among the rest of the populace by the fact of their being held longer. Regardless of the ending of the operation, the Crisis Staff gave its agreement that the municipal Territorial Defence Staff that these persons should undergo interrogation for selection and then be evacuated from the stadium." And then it deals with a conclusion, the 4th of May, which I'm not going to deal with at the moment. A few brief questions about this. First of all, it's right, isn't it - I'm sure I can lead on this - that it was presupposed at that time by the Crisis Staff that four days was going to be a long time for detention?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a long time period, as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the high costs aspects? What was that referring to? Obviously food and lodging speaks for itself in one sense. What about the reference to high costs of security?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this has been incorrectly translated. It's not the costs of security. It was about costs, and if we know the situation, if we know that at that time the overall area of Bosanska Krajina there was a sort of ghetto block, there was a danger of an economic nature. We had no communication because of the war in Croatia, and because of the interruptions with respect to Serbia. So we were in an encirclement in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If any answer is based on the assumption that the translation is not correct, it should be checked rather than to allow a witness to proceed without verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That must be right, Your Honour, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless we are close to -- if you finish your sentence, your last sentence was that you said that you were in an encirclement. Let me just repeat your one last sentence where I stopped you. Then invite to you finish it and then we'll have a break. You said -- you explained that there was a sort of ghetto block, there was a danger of an economic nature, we had no communication because of the war in Croatia, and because of the interruptions with respect to Serbia, so we were in an encirclement in a way. That was part of your explanation of the text we will look at more closely. Please finish your answer. So you were in an encirclement in a way and then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to say what the meaning of this report was, the sense of it, written in this form because it was assessed at the time that there weren't enough food supplies, food stocks, and other necessities, if you were somewhere else or located somewhere. So we asked that if there was information from the TO headquarters and staffs that these were sort of extremists and that they were interesting for processing purposes, that this should be done quickly and effectively and if -- and the ones, the suspects for which there were no grounds to hold them should be left straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. We'll adjourn. May I first ask, Madam Usher, you to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse how much time do you still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to be at least an hour, perhaps nearer two, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness was scheduled for four hours. The Chamber is not unaware that it took quite some time itself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not so much that, my excuse or, more seriously, my explanation is in fact this Crisis Staff document and, of course, I did not realise until I got this translation, how significant it would be. We must spent I hope there is no criticism of this, at least three hours on it, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's an interesting document, although the witness also testified that publication of this document might have influenced some of the language, or at least. But could I just learn from the Registrar -- I think one more hour, then would you have, apart from that, some of the questions of the Judges, of course, add to the information already, but one more hour would bring you over four hours. So would you please try to finish within the first hour after the break. Let's see how far we come, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I expect you will --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will try my best. I have been the first to concede on every occasion that my personal estimates are guesstimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes for the better, sometimes for the worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate that. You're expected to do your utmost best to finish within the hour and, if that's not possible, then please demonstrate during that hour that you're using your time as efficiently as possible. And -- for example, a lot of time spending on colour photographs, on a CD, which could be -- and then finally, if I asked, "Does it add anything," then the answer is no. So under those circumstances you could have discussed with Mr. Harmon whether he would be in need of having nice colours or not. I mean, I'm talking about these kinds of things. Let's proceed. We will adjourn and -- for the interpreters, I was informed that another team will assist us the afternoon. Otherwise I would not have dared to go on for such a long time. We will adjourn until a quarter past 2. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on a bit in the bundle. We are still at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to what we think is P141, which is a letter that you sent to civil affairs HQ headquarters in Topusko, in effect Mr. Kirudja, dated the 6th of July of 1992. Now, I don't know whether you can help us with this. We can see that there is a B/C/S version of this document that purports to be signed, bearing your name. There is also an English version which is clearly an original document, and then there is also an English translation, an official translation. First question is: Do you remember anything about the English translation? Who sorted that out, why did you send it, anything along those lines?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember for certain who translated this letter. I am really unable to remember precisely whether anyone was asked to do this by the municipal authorities or whether this was done in a different way. I can't say because I don't remember. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember sending the letter at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, there were certain letters being sent. There were conversations that were conducted. Some of it was done in writing. I can't remember specifically when or how. I do remember there being letters, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was your aim in reducing the subject matter of this particular letter to writing?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one reads through this document, I believe at the bottom of the page, if you look at the second-last passage, you can see what the letter itself explains. It explains that something had been agreed already. I believe we are at a point in time here when I had already talked to the representatives of that committee. I believe we should be able to conclude that based on this letter, that it had been agreed, as a matter of principle, to give assistance to the Muslim population so that they could leave the area. An order had been given that security should be provided for the buses about to leave the area over the following days and then certain company names are given, companies that would take charge of this. I think this letter talks about the agreement that we reached with the people from Topusko or rather from the UNPROFOR base at Dvor Na Uni.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like you to have a look at a document that is not in the bundle but I think has been handed out. It bears a -- front page is an UNPROFOR message form dated the 13th of July of 1992, and as far as we can make out, Your Honour, this is P145. And it's not the message form itself I'd like you to look at. It's the memorandum. To state the obvious the original is in English so you have got a translation. And it talks about 20 busloads of refugees from Bosanski Novi crossing the border towards Croatian-controlled territory through sector north. I will read it, "Today an advance group of people from Bosanski Novi arrived at the gate of Dancon in Dvor and announced that on Wednesday, 15th July--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "Today an advanced group of people from Bosanski Novi arrived at the gate of Dancon in Dvor and announced that on Wednesday, 15 July, at 12 noon, 20 busloads of refugees will arrive in Dvor. The people have been advised that UNPROFOR will not be in a position to assist them in crossing and the government of Croatia has given instructions to its border police not to accept their entry into Croatian-controlled territory. We appreciate it if the humanitarian agencies concerned could be alerted and coordinate appropriate action in UNPA north with UNPROFOR." As far as you can remember, what actually happened on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have already indicated, some principles had been agreed in terms of how the operation would unfold, how all the people would leave Novi Grad municipality, the modalities, and this is something that had preceded the meetings that I had been talking about. I've tried to explain this in a way. I don't know about this letter that is referred to here but I know about this moment when people had already begun to talk about these columns. I have no reason not to believe that this was the 15th of July. So once the columns had been formed, this group reached the bridge that you saw in that photograph. The UNPROFOR forces stopped there and blocked passage to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which is now Croatia. Those people, the UNPROFOR people, told us that they could not allow the convoy to pass because the Croatian authorities disagreed and refused to give authorisation for their passage across that stretch of land between Croatia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. May I follow through on this or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. If you go on, please, I'd like you to describe literally what happened to these refugees on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened sometime in the afternoon, when those people were stopped. I was there. I attended the negotiations. I continued to be there. I was told that I could not take that crossing to Topusko to Tusilovici or on to Karlovac for that matter. That was the area separating the Republic of Krajina and the Republic of Croatia. We were there for two or three hours. I can't be more specific, just standing, waiting for a letter that was supposed to arrive from, if my understanding was correct, some people who were superior to UNPROFOR. I'm not sure if they were in Zagreb or elsewhere. Apparently they had been engaged in talks searching for an opportunity to cross into Croatia. In my understanding, they were having talks with both people from the Croatian government and someone from UNPROFOR. We waited for about two or three hours after which they explained that we would be allowed to cross but not over that bridge. They said we should take our column a bit further back down the Bosnian side as far as Bosnian Dubica. They said we should go to another crossing near Bosanska Dubica called Jasenovac. A bridge had been destroyed there. There had been a bridge there before the war. They said they would erect some sort of a raft or a pontoon bridge for us to cross the river. The column was then redirected and headed for Dubica. However, at the crossing itself between Kotoriste Grad and Kotorska Dubica, the municipal authorities stopped us and for a -- for some reason I did not know, refused to allow us to pass through Kotorska Dubica. Again we found ourselves facing an inconvenient situation. What were we to do with all those people since we could no longer go back? But I think it was I who proposed for us all to go back to Kostajnica, the distance being some 15 kilometres, to back track, as it were, to see if it was possible to cross there, to allow throws people to cross over to Hrvatska Kostajnica and onwards. I remember well there was an UNPROFOR base in Kostajnica. Again I met some people there. I can't remember who. Anyway, those people told me we would have to wait a while to see what would happen. The convoy stayed on the Bosnian side in Bosanska Kostajnica and the UNPROFOR was on the Croatian side in Croatian Kostajnica. These two towns are separated by the river Una. This took a long time, until midnight or possibly 1.00 in the morning. I know that at the time those people who secured the convoy, in a way, who provided our security, came over and told me that there was a real danger since this was night time, those people were there in Kostajnica in their cars and vehicles, that there was a real danger of an incident occurring, yet again another column being attacked by someone. It was night time and therefore it was very difficult to make sure that nothing happened. We agreed that all the people -- that all the people should head back to their homes regardless of how long the negotiations would take. It was taking too long, especially as far as the UNPROFOR people in Kostajnica were concerned. They sent us back to Novi Grad, and all those people, between the 15th of July and for about one week after the 15th of July, these people headed back to their homes and stayed there waiting for the situation to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So to state the obvious, the convoy of buses had been arranged and the people had obviously got into the buses and then the buses had taken the route that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As you say, people on the buses, the Bosniaks, all went back home. What about the occupants of the football stadium? Had they joined the buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
