utterances.text: I really can't remember for certain. I have no reliable recollection of that. I just know that all those people were sent back. I have no idea if they came back once more later on. I can't remember right now. But I do think that some of those, as I've said before, the best part of the people at the stadium were already staying in houses around town, wherever it was even relatively safe. I can't remember specifically whether people were sent back from that particular convoy, people from the Mlavke football stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The problems that you have just described, the buses, for want of a better expression, encountered, how were these problems overcome in the next week or so before the convoy actually left Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations continued, and that is how the problems were overcome. I'm not sure where the negotiations took place. I think it was in Dvor Na Uni in the UNPROFOR base. They were looking for the same solution, at least that's what they told us. They said they would be dealing with the problems very soon. They said they were sorry that the whole thing happened the way they did. The people were tired. They knew that. They had spent the entire day on the buses. They said they would do everything within their power to deal with this matter so that those people could go wherever they close to go. That is what they told us during our talks. I think this was on the 21st, 2nd, or 3rd of July. As you see, I'm in the very specific about this. The convoy was reorganised, as it were, and those people left on the same day, in conditions of perfect safety. If you look at that letter which talks about the buses, and the companies, they used those. And those who had their own cars or vehicles could use those. Nobody stood in the way. They were free to leave in their own cars, if they so wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By -- you mean the letter of P141, your letter of the 6th of July? From the page in English?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we discussed the letter a while ago. So that's the one I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's just be precise about it, if we may. It's your letter of the 6th of July 1992, that describes -- mentions the two companies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go back to the photographs for a moment, please? The last photograph. What does this photograph depict, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this photograph, we can see the buses on the day that the convoy was organised under the auspices of UNPROFOR. I think you can see an UNPROFOR vehicle here sporting a flag. They were monitoring the process whereby the Muslim population was leaving the Novi Grad area. This was the day when the agreement was finally reached, and they assumed upon themselves the responsibility to see the population out, I mean UNPROFOR and the refugee committee based in Topusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's clear from the colour photograph, for what it's worth, that that is a blue, United Nations flag on the United Nations vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know whereabouts this photograph was taken? In other words what countryside this depicts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was given these photographs by some foreign journalists. They said this was somewhere between Dvor Na Uni municipality and Mlin which used to be part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and is now part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to fully understand that, this picture is not taken on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or what was then -- what is now Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At least the way the journalists told me, or rather the photograph. At this point, these people were already on their way out and this shows them some way along the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just not to misunderstand. You said these people were already on their way out. From what you just told us, I would phrase that as that they had left already the territory of your municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not sure I understand your question. What exactly do you mean by "on their way out"? Out of where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's how it was translated to us. If I say, "I'm on had my way out," I understand that to be, but I'm not a native English-speaker, that I'm on the way to leave the location which is mentioned, where I do understand from your testimony that these buses had already left the territory of your municipality according to what the journalist told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This photograph was not taken in Novi Grad municipality. What I was told is that this was a snapshot of the convoy just a small portion of the convoy photographed between Novi Grad and Karlovac. More specifically somewhere around Dvor municipality and Glina municipality. They were en route, and that's when this photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, we have now three times asked the question. Do you understand the answer to be that it was not on the territory of the witness's municipality any more, so they had left and were still on their way to whatever destination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's how I understood his evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The occupants of the football stadium, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people at the football stadium were also in this convoy and they left together with the other people, those who wished to leave the territory of Novi Grad. So all of them left together, those who had remained at the stadium left together with others going in that direction. After that, based on what I know, there were no people left on the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps for completeness I should have asked you this: It's right, isn't it, that eventually the buses did in fact cross the bridge, the bridge that we see in the photographs -- the bridge that you're standing on in the photographs that were taken some weeks earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at tab 4? This is a document that's helpfully in both of our languages. Where it says date or datum at the bottom, what date do you read?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this document is in English. In Serbian, in the last line, it says, place, Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The date immediately above that, please, which is written in manuscript?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that this is 8, but I'm not quite sure. Then slash 10, and then slash again, and then 1992. If I read can out correctly. It's not entirely clear to me, the first digit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, we can see that this relates to 1560 people who were -- will be transferred from Bosanski Novi to Karlovac. Are you able to help us at all as to which people this document is referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that this document doesn't look familiar to me. I also don't know that anything else was organised after this convoy. I don't know that anybody departed in an organised manner. Therefore, I can't give you any further information regarding this document. It doesn't look familiar to me, and doesn't ring a bell, so to say. Looking at this document, even the signature that is right below the first stamp, Cedomir Aleksic, even that is not familiar to me. All I know is that after this organised departure, in which UNPROFOR took part and the UNHCR, as far as I know, nothing else was done in the following period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the name, Dr. Cedomir Aleksic, is that name familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said to you, I don't know this person. The name doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure under the rules, Your Honour, whether this then can become an exhibit. I'm not inviting it to. I don't -- I'm entirely neutral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, of course, the evidence is that this witness doesn't know about the name and about the document. We could admit it to a limited extent. One of the other ways of dealing with it is to mark it for identification so that at least we know what the witness didn't know, although the name is on it. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My inclination, Your Honour, would be to mark it for identification only.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm more than content with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification and it will bear number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D117, MFI, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D117, MFI. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You in fact only remained president of the municipal assembly until the end of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Literally in a sentence, if you can, why did you cease to be president?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say there were several reasons. One of the main reasons was that I myself was not happy with the existing situation with all the terrible things and misfortunes that had taken place. It was very difficult for me to work under those conditions. And perhaps it was cowardly of me to resign. Perhaps people view it through that prism as well. There was really not much I could do. My authorities were very limited and the responsibilities placed on the shoulder of the president of municipality were huge while at the same time, as I've said already, the president did not have wide enough authorities to fulfil the responsibility. This is not how it looked to the public but that's how it was. Therefore, I took that position because I believed that under the circumstances I did not wish and I was not able to continue to do that work. There was too much burden tying me down, and at the same time, my hands were tied and I was -- I didn't have sufficient authorities to deal with the amount of problems I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, at the point of the departure of the Bosniaks from your municipality, were you aware of any maltreatment of them at the hands of Serbs whilst they were in detention at the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were at the football stadium, as far as I know, were not mistreated. Nobody harassed them, attacked them physically or insulted them in any other way. They were not subjected to any mistreatment. As I've already stated here, there were certain cases of outbursts and even killings committed by the paramilitaries. Trials were launched against these people and you can find information about this in courts in Novi Grad and in the high court in Banja Luka. I think that the basic court, a municipal court, could issue sentences up to ten years, and everything more serious than that was handled by the Banja Luka court. And based on the documents and records existing there, you can see that trials were instituted against these people, these people who committed crimes in order to acquire personal gain, who committed killings and so on. I'm not aware of all of the information regarding these cases but I know that there were trials and I know that this was handled in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I don't know whether that would be your next question. When took these trials place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not really competent to discuss court proceedings. However, I know of a case -- I remember it well because I knew the person who was killed. I think that he was a criminal inspector. He worked at the police station, and he was killed sometime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I was just asking about when, not what case exactly. If we would like to know. I'll ask you. So when took these trials place? Was that still in 1992? Were the people arrested immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I was going to say. Five days after the murder, the perpetrators, the killers, were caught. They were detained, placed in detention, and then trial was launched. I don't know what course the trial had, but all I know is that immediately upon discovering that a murder had been committed, a trial was instituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The victim was of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The victim was a Muslim, and the murderer was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many of these cases, in your recollection, were taken to court? Five, ten, 20, a hundred? Could you give us an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly wouldn't be able to give you the number. I know that there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about trials, but when did those trials take place, and what were the crimes investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't quite understand your question. Would you elaborate on it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier on, you told us that there was chaos, you told us that there were a lot of mistreatments for the civilian population, you told us that houses were looted, you told us that murders were committed, and I asked you a question, and you answered in the following way. You told us there was such a chaos that the police couldn't do much, it was too much for everyone, and now you're talking, you're telling us -- you're talking about trials, about multiple trials, and I would like to know when these crimes took place, when did these crimes take place? Were there different incidents? And I'm thinking about the incidents that you mentioned this morning. So for these trials were the incidents different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that police was helpless, was unable to do anything. Police did something. But not sufficient in order to establish full law and order. Therefore, police did take some steps and one of such cases was that after five days, they were able to find the murderer. So one cannot really say that police did nothing. They did take certain steps. These people were brought to trial. However, in my view, that wasn't sufficient, that wasn't sufficient to consider their work as satisfactory. So to repeat, police did take certain steps but not full measures in order to preserve law and order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, you are not just talking about one case, the case that you have mentioned, i.e. this person who was arrested five days after a murder. You are telling us that there were several cases and that there was a follow-up, and that there were several trials. Do you agree with me there were several trials, several people who were brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes, yes. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So presumably we will be able to find in the Court archives the minutes of these trials, and the sentencing as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. One should be able to find the records. I know that archives are there in place, that records should be there. So all of these facts could be located. One could establish exactly how many trials there were. I myself know that there were several but I do not know the exact number. What I'm trying to tell you is that there were different crimes committed. However, I focused on the cases in which Serbs were the perpetrators and Muslims unfortunately were the victims. So I just told you about the cases that were instituted during this period of time, that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question in this respect. You said the perpetrator of this murder was arrested after five days. Was this a murder that was perpetrated in the -- well, let's say the Japra valley event, so mid-May? Was it at that occasion that this person was murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that this was roughly in late June or early July. I'm not quite sure. I think it was during that period of time. The man who was killed lived somewhere in town. I don't know his exact address. However, this could be checked, either at the police station or in court records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the other cases you were talking about, could you with certainty locate these cases in time and in place in the context of the Japra valley event, as we have discussed that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood your question well, you wanted to know whether any proceedings were instituted against people who committed certain crimes in the Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, ones you mentioned killings, arson, all the -- let's say the cruel events that have been described in this report as well. Is there anyone arrested and prosecuted, punished and sentenced for crimes committed in that specific context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that an investigation was conducted during that period of time, and certain proceedings. As far as I know, during that period of time, in 1992, upon discovering that certain people were perpetrators, and I don't think that this was completed quickly, I think that the proceedings progressed through 1993 and 1994. I don't know what the final outcome was. But I'm sure that this information could be located in the Court in Novi Grad or in the high court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know of any perpetrator being arrested for any of these crimes committed during what I call the Japra valley event, that is the event which is described in the report, on the specific dates? Do you know of any specific perpetrator being arrested for one of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell me, could you please tell me when and do you have any further details? So, first, when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to give you the exact period of time, but it was roughly then, between May and perhaps August of 1992. I don't know the exact dates, though. I can't remember. I know that these paramilitary formations and small groups which were active there and committed crimes, among them there was one comprising people who had been criminals even before the war. They were called Suva Rebra, the people who were in that group were called Petici and Djukic, and they did stand trial. I don't know the exact date. However, I know that there was a trial, they were prosecuted, an investigation was conducted, and trial followed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were prosecuted for crimes committed during this Japra valley event or for any criminal -- or were they prosecuted for any criminal behaviour outside of that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't go as far as to qualify the crime. I know that a crime was committed and that people were prosecuted. As to how exactly the crime was legally qualified, I wouldn't be able to tell you. It was up to the court and I don't know whether they qualified it correctly or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you for that. I asked whether they were prosecuted for any crime committed during these couple of days where these horrible things happened in the Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said to you that they were prosecuted and that there was a trial, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you still do not answer my question. My question is: Was -- were the charges brought against these persons for crimes committed during these couple of days described in the report what happened in Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I misunderstood your question. Let me repeat. There was a trial. The trial was not instituted immediately. Trials probably were instituted as the crimes were uncovered and as the situation became more stable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, why don't you answer my question? My question is quite simple. Were they prosecuted, were they charged, for any of the crimes committed during these couple of days in the events in Japra valley or were they charged with perhaps crimes committed elsewhere at another moment? That's my question. And I've put it now five times to you, so I would rather like to receive an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really did not understand your question initially. However, I've understood it now. Naturally, yes, trials were held for crimes committed. Trials in cases where the perpetrators were Serbs and Muslims were the victims. It was not only in the Japra valley. It was all over the region, in town as well, and as I've said to you already, there were such crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did the charges comprise events in the Japra valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat, not only in the Japra valley but in the entire region. Some crimes were committed in the Japra valley. However, some were committed in town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the crimes committed in the Japra valley were committed, the people were charged with those crimes as they were committed during these couple of days you described in the report; is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In places where evidence existed, where facts were uncovered, proceedings were instituted even when the perpetrator's identity was not known. The organs tried to locate the perpetrators and in some cases they were not able to discover who had committed certain crimes but, in some cases, yes, and in those cases, people stood trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I've tried for ten minutes to get an answer which I would consider certainly in favour of the accused, that Prosecutions were instituted against those who had participated in the crimes committed during this Japra valley operation. I give it up now but if you have any better chance, then please try. I was really seeking this, as you may have noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, but I'm also addressing you, Mr. Harmon, as you may have noticed from the line of questions, the Chamber considers itself potential relevance to know it. And so therefore, is there any documentation -- if there is any documentation available the Chamber would like to receive that so that we get concrete answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's going to make what I'm about to say that much easier. Your Honour, the position is this: That the witness, as the Court is vaguely aware but I'm now going to make it specifically aware, was interviewed in June of 2003. Now, Mr. Harmon provided me with that interview as a courtesy, and he made it quite clear to me that it was as a courtesy. I think he accepted, and he is there to speak for himself in a moment, but some of it may have been -- he may have had to have provided it under Rule 68 but he effectively decided to give it all to me, my having requested it after my recent trip and having spoken to this gentleman and learned that he had in fact been interviewed. I was quite anxious to put this interview before the court for a variety of reasons. Mr. Harmon dissuaded me not to do. Its admissibility may have been in some doubt. He's asked about this at some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He is asked about this in the interview. I certainly want that passage to go before the Court and, in addition to that, could I make this comment? He's asked about it, he gives some answers, and I'm very anxious to know what the investigators, OTP investigators, indeed there was an OTP lawyer there, have done about the information the witness provided. I'm sorry to spring that on Mr. Harmon but at one point I was thinking of asking for a short adjournment because he and I have had quite lengthy discussions about this matter, and Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn for one second to private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes we are in open.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before I sit down, what I was in the middle of saying, and it's important, I accept that this is a matter of sensitivity to my learned friend, and he and I have had quite long and at times marginally difficult conversations about this particular topic. And I'm sorry that I've had to raise it now without having had a chance to speak to him further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, any comment? I must say that if we are talking about an interview that I hope questions and answers in that interview were better linked than they were over the last ten minutes. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, during the next recess counsel and I could discuss this matter and we could try to resolve this matter. My second observation is, Your Honour, we submitted in our case in chief evidence in respect of Prosecutions, a considerable volume of evidence. I won't comment on that now. But there was considerable evidence in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to review that. I hope you don't mind that we don't have it all in our memory actively available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am actually getting near the end of my examination. Clearly I'm going to need to take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I would request that the Court go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to ask you a few questions in relation to him, please. Firstly, the best of your recollection, did you see him, have a meeting with him, or have any dealings with him in Bosanski Novi in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, and to the extent that I'm familiar with this, there were no meetings or conversations with Mr. Krajisnik in Bosanski Novi at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1992, do you recall a meeting where a large number of Bosnian Serb leaders were in attendance, as well as leaders from the neighbouring Serb Krajina republic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the meeting of the assembly. I think that's what it was called, the Joint Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. This took place in Novi Grad but it was not back in 1992. Rather, it was sometime in April or May, the spring of 1993, at least as far as I can remember. This meeting of the assembly was held in Novi Grad. That much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it may again be obvious but I think I should ask you, the events that you have described in relation to the various problems in the Japra valley and in particular the departure of the Bosniaks and your negotiations with UNPROFOR, did Mr. Krajisnik play any part in those at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did not. I think there was this once when the telephone lines were re-established, because, as I have said, there had been a total communication breakdown at one point with the republican leadership. I think once he called me on the phone, and I think members of the Serbian Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, were there too. I spoke to one of them. I can't remember which one. But they just wanted to get some general background on the situation that prevailed in our municipality. There were no specific proposals being made or instructions being given. This was purely for information purposes, nothing else, and nothing followed. This conversation gave rise to nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I invite the Court to take an early break? I wish to speak to my learned friend and wish to leave open this examination until I have done that and also have a word with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please. Yes. If you have a conversation with Mr. Krajisnik as well, with the last witness we were confronted with a wish of Mr. Krajisnik to add any questions to questions put to the witness by counsel. That was done only when the witness was re-examined, which seems not to be the right moment to take such an initiative. So if you consult with Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Josse, would you also try to find out whether any additional questions, of course, preferably to the put to the witness by you, but -- well, it now and then happens, not very often, that for one reason or another, it's preferred by the Defence that Mr. Krajisnik puts the question. If that's the case, would you also give the necessary guidance to Mr. Krajisnik not to lead, et cetera, et cetera. So if you would please include that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got some reasonably good news for the Court. He and I had a discussion during the last adjournment. I think we see eye to eye on this. It's belt and braces on my part that I would like to speak to him again. Most of my time is going to, I suspect, be taken up with Mr. Harmon rather than my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then clear. We will then have a break until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that it's right, I think, to say that we have not come to an agreement. However, for reasons, as I've said, that I don't propose or wish to go into I'm not going to argue the point and seek any form of ruling. What my learned friend has agreed that I can do, and in the absence of an agreement as far as the document is concerned, this is what I propose to do, is lead in relation to the passages and names that the witness mentioned in the course of the interview. So that's what I propose to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom again. And do you have any idea, it's not easy to give an assessment, do you have any idea of time how much this will take us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This exercise will take I imagine five to ten minutes, and then I will be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, a few more questions will be put to you by Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, when you were interviewed in June of 2003 by a Paul Grady, a Julian Nicholls, and a Timothy Resch, you were -- various questions were put to you over the course of the day in Banja Luka. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think it's right, and probably important to mention, the fact that you were cautioned that you were being treated as a suspect. That was the purpose of the interview, so you were told?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as I've already said the interview took the best, really the whole day and, in effect, within the last couple of pages, they almost ran out of time and said that they might be in contact with you again. I don't think they ever did contact you again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it's also fair and right to point out that they offered you a lawyer and you chose not to have a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Towards the end of the interview when it was clear from what was being said that time was running short you were asked about court proceedings that had taken place, as a result of some of the crimes that you had described. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And rather like you told this Court, you told the interviewers that they could check the documents in Novi Grad basic court and the district court in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned a Zoran Dukic and a Mladen Dukic who had committed a crime, I think you say for the theft of two cows from a Muslim, Mohamed Kuzmetovic [phoen]. And I'll go on. You went on and said there was -- proceedings were instigated and he was convicted. "I don't know how many months, but he was. I'm talking about property, let's go, let me just find my bearings here." And then in fact, Mr. Resch interrupted you and asked you if you could deal with Article 36, manslaughter, Article 38, serious bodily injury, and indeed, "better yet," he says, "war crimes." And you say, "Let me finish. Murder of Hotic Husein, 1 July 1992, this is the time when the Muslims had already left for Doboj but not to Croatia yet." Who murdered -- "who murdered Husein Hotic," Mr. Resch asked you. And then it says, rather unfortunately, the English that I have reads, "Witness lists names in B/C/S, not translated." Then it says "Petic Goran, Dukic Goran, Dukic Mladen, Baron Dragoljub." So these four men were brought in as suspects. Now, I've mentioned to you quite a lot of names there. Two Dukic's, someone called Petic, somebody probably called Baron. There is a question mark by his name in English. Two victims, a Husein Hotic and a Mohamed Kuzmetovic does any of that jog your memory and, if so, tell us how it jogs your memory, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the statement I gave. I think the only error is when you mentioned the names, you said Dukic. It probably should have been Djukic. I had been asked or at least that was my understanding of the question at the time about proceedings and it was suggested that no proceedings had been instituted and that no Serb perpetrators had been punished or that there was no will to have any of them punished. I was trying to show some of the case that is were documented and real. The examples that you have listed are a handful but there are more of those. This is correct. And this is the same thing that I have been speaking about. I can't remember the exact date now but I think you mentioned the 1st of July, and that should be accurate. I think it was four or five days later that the perpetrators were arrested and prosecuted, the murderers, the names that you have read out. The record of that trial or those trials should be available and you can probably obtain that from the basic court or from the Banja Luka district court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- of course, I do understand that you seek to establish that prosecutions were taking place. The Chamber was very much interested, at least I was, about the Japra valley -- well, operation, not in the military sense but at least the events in Japra valley. 1st of July was far after the Japra valley event, a couple of weeks. Do you remember where this person was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already indicated, that was the very person that I had in mind. I think it was in the vicinity of the town but I don't know exactly. There should be a document indicating the exact place where this person was murdered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's unrelated to the events in the Japra valley. At least not directly related to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how this case could be viewed separately. All these things had to do with Novi Grad municipality. I didn't draw any conclusions there myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think the Chamber did. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For completeness, you in fact were then asked by Mr. Nicholls what was the sentence and you said, "On 5th July they were taken, they were taken in for four days. There was an investigation. They were put on trial. So the Crisis Staff, whenever they were able to establish the circumstances, they were trying to get the SJB to take those people into court to be processed." And you were asked whether you knew the sentence and you said you didn't know, you can check in the basic court. And on two occasions, Mr. Nicholls said we will check that. We'll look that up. I think it's fair to say that you were not asked specifically about the Japra valley. The Chamber sees what you're trying to say about the connection between the events, the unfortunate killing of Mr. Husein and the Japra valley events. Do you have any recollection of any investigation into the events in the Japra valley before the Muslims left that area?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I have pointed this out already. I'm not sure whether I was clear enough. There were things being done. I'm not sure when exactly, but proceedings had been instituted. There were a great number of perpetrators, and there was an attempt to establish who the perpetrators were, to get their names. I cannot say what stage the proceedings reached but I can tell you what the public security station informed me about. They told me that there were people on the ground, that the crime police were doing their work, the operative work, and that they would keep me posted on whatever they found. This process was underway and continuing at a difficult time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to leave it there, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Pasic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm waiting, Your Honour, until the packages are distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you could start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thanks very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the witness could be first of all presented with Defence Exhibit I believe it's 116, 115, a copy of the report on the work of the Crisis Staff that we discussed this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, I just want to go over very quickly and I think you can help us with this, resolve an ambiguity that appears within this particular report. It references two Crisis Staffs. Page 1 of the English translation of this, the first, at the top of page 1 of the B/C/S version, it discusses in its original form the Crisis Staff was formed essentially at the beginning of April, at the request, on the proposal of higher SDS organs. You testified about that. And when asked, approximately, could you give us greater details about that, the formation of the Crisis Staff, you were not particularly able to give us greater details about what gave rise to the formation of the Crisis Staff. I know you are aware of variant B and variant B document and you had seen that document at some point in time prior to the creation of the Crisis Staff that's described in April of 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is quite long. I don't know if I understood it right. Could you please repeat the actual question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the document referred to as variant A and variant B?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have the same document in mind, we just spoke about the interview that I gave in Banja Luka, and in that case, if that's what you have in mind, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's be perfectly clear on what I have in mind so if you have the documents in front of you, Mr. Pasic, do you have a set of documents in front of you? That will be presented to you and I'm going to refer you to tab 38. Just if you would cast an eye on that document, Mr. Pasic, that's the document I have in mind. That's the document you were asked about on an earlier occasion.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is familiar. I think that this part is complete. I can't read all of it now but I assume that this is right, and Variant A and B that we covered during my interview is something that I am familiar with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Variant A and Variant B document, as you are aware, Variant A which dealt with municipalities where there was a majority of Serbs called for the establishment of Crisis Staffs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about the same document now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think my learned friend can assert that with respect. The witness needs to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was trying to get through this because I thought he was familiar with this. But I will be glad to take him through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is about the same document. The witness just said that it looked familiar to him when looking at it, familiar to the extent that it looked like the document that was presented to him during his interview. That's how I understood. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pasic, if you turn in this document, in the B/C/S, let me read a portion of Variant A and Variant B to you. It says, under Variant A, under the first level, this is on page 3 of the English translation, unfortunately it's in Cyrillic and I cannot direct you to the specific portion but let me read it to you, Mr. Pasic. The first level under subpart 3 it says, "SDS municipal boards shall immediately -- shall establish immediately Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in the municipality composed of the following." And then it lists a group of persons. My only interest in this, Mr. Pasic, don't want to spend a lot of time on this, was that Variant A and Variant B document that you were familiar with called for the establishment of Crisis Staffs in Serb-majority municipalities, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't give a yes or no answer. As I said to you, Variant A and B, as they are called, is something that I am familiar with. This document in a way gives instructions on how and when to establish Crisis Staffs. Novi Grad municipality had no need to establish a Crisis Staff in that period of time, when this document was issued. If I may continue, I can give you more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I want you to carefully listen to the questions and to answer to the questions, and if any further detail is needed, you'll be asked for it. As a matter of fact, Mr. Harmon was drawing your attention to page 2 of the B/C/S version of this document, tab 38, at -- relatively at the top of the page, under 3, Mr. Harmon asked you whether this document called for the establishment of Crisis Staffs in Serb-majority municipalities, yes or no. So he's just asking about what this document calls for. Would you agree with him or would you disagree with him that this document calls for the establishment of Crisis Staffs at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what it calls for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, on February 14th you attended in Sarajevo at the holiday an extended session of the main board and the executive board of the SDS at which time level 2 of those particular instructions, Variant A and Variant B were called to be implemented by Radovan Karadzic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't remember whether I attended that meeting. I did attend some meetings but right now I can't claim whether I attended precisely this meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to turn to tab 39, Mr. Pasic. Tab 39 are the -- is a transcript of that particular meeting, and I want to direct your attention and I want to direct the Court's attention to four passages. Perhaps this will refresh your recollection. I'm referring first, Mr. Pasic, and Your Honours, to page 5 of the English version at the bottom, line 32, and, Mr. Pasic, for your benefit, in the B/C/S version I'm referring to the page that has in the up ever right-hand corner numbers 04002200. I'm going to read very slowly from the middle of the page that you should be looking at the following passage and I'm going to read you four passages before I ask to you comment and I would like you then to comment. The first passage I've directed your attention to reads as follows: "That is, if you remember who keeps that in mind, or maybe not on his person, a stage number 2. There is -- remember you know what I am talking about, we know, yes, that is therefore the stage number 2, the second stage in smaller or bigger variations, but you have to implement that slowly now, to have absolute control who is travelling along your roads, what they are transporting, for which purposes. That's the way it must be. You have to have at your disposal, first of all, you have to have a -- have legal organs, reserve police and regular police which has to carry out their duties on orders of a -- civil authorities because you are civil authorities in most municipalities, in large number of municipalities, in all our municipalities, it is you." Now the second passage, Mr. Pasic, I would like to direct your attention to and the Court's attention, Your Honours, I'm referring to the English version page 7, lines 11 through 15, and Mr. Pasic, I'm referring to the very next page, 0400-2201, at the middle of the page, and I will read again a portion of Dr. Karadzic's statement. "The second thing that is very important, it gives us full moral right not to accept any decision resulting from the referendum, and it gives us the right to introduce the stage number 2 in functioning of your areas, and relaying [sic] on your own forces to absolutely defend yourselves from the independent Bosnia and Hercegovina." The third passage I would like to quote Dr. Karadzic is found at page 24 in the English version, Mr. Pasic, and in the version that is in front of you, the B/C/S version, it's at 0400-2208. It appears at the lower quarter of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour, had a slightly dud copy. I took it over because mine is now -- stops at page 22 so perhaps I could swap with the Registry copy for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the passage from Dr. Karadzic. "And as regards the essence of which Mr. Radic spoke, now, please, that is why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level, and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." I'm sorry, Mr. Pasic, that's my mistake but let me -- that, Your Honours was found at page 24 of the English and Mr. Pasic, just for your benefit, that is found -- bear with me, Mr. Pasic. Let me start again, Mr. Pasic. I'd like to direct your attention and the Court's attention to page 17 of the English, lines 14 through 18, and, Mr. Pasic, for your benefit, that is found at 0400-2208, at the bottom third of the page, and that quotation, Mr. Pasic, reads as follows: "There is nothing that we shall disapprove of except for foolish things and I think that we Serbs must stop with declarations, with declaration. We have had enough declarations and now those declarations should be translated into a map and the stage number 2 should also be converted, the one we've talked about, the one you have, if not here, then at home." And finally, Mr. Pasic, I will reread to you the passage I read before that is found in the English version at page 24, lines 20 through 23, and in the B/C/S passage found at 0400-2210. And that's found in the middle of the page, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have in mind 01 or 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I said 2201, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 24 would then be earlier than page 17, which is surprising, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, is correct, I'm sorry. 2214 is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Pasic, that's found at the top of page 2214. So let me read this to you. "And as regards the essence of which Mr. Radic spoke, now, please, that is why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." Mr. Pasic, does that refresh your recollection as to whether you attended this particular session of the extended session of the main board and executive board of the SDS held on the 14th of February 1992 in Sarajevo at the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what has been read out, I still cannot make any claims. I do not remember whether I was present. I don't know whether there are some -- any additional details and whether that could refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me try to refresh your memory a different way, Mr. Pasic. If we could turn to tab 40, there should be two documents at tab 40. The first document, Mr. Pasic, is a document which I will read a portion of into the record. It says, "Bill number 05294/2, 158166 to be paid for hotel services for members of SDS assembly for 14th and 15th February 1992," and if you turn to the second document, Mr. Pasic, second document, do you have that in front of you, Mr. Pasic? That exhibit? The second document is a -- reads, "Holiday Inn hotel, name, R. Pasic-Dejanovic, SDS, price 5.000 for room 631/1, arrival February 14th and it bears a receipt number 0018541." Mr. Pasic, does that assist you in recalling whether or not you attended this session of the main board that I referred to in the Holiday Inn on the 14th of February?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I still do not remember. You have to admit that it's been a long time. I truly do not remember all of the sessions and meetings. I think that I already stated this once. I know that certain sessions were held. I know that I attended some of them. But whether it was precisely this one held on this day, I don't know. What you just read out to me did not refresh my memory, and I cannot claim with any certainty that I was present. Once again, I don't remember all of those events and the texts that we have read out today do not help me remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One final question on the receipt that bears your name and the name of another person, Dejanovic. Who was Mr. Dejanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there were two men called Dejanovic, if we are talking about the Serbian democratic party. There was Milos Dejanovic and Mirko Dejanovic. I don't know which one is mentioned here. I can't remember after 15 years or 13 years. I can't remember which one was present and who I met with at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember sharing a room with Mr. Dejanovic in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let me then turn to tab 42. I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm a bit confused about tab 40 because I do not see any original from the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, one of our two copies that we now have had it and the other had a considerable number of reproductions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take care that we get. I have received now a translation of something which seems to be addressed to the SDS BiH and we have an original, but the original only addresses R. Pasic-Dejanovic. Could any of the persons by the name of Dejanovic, Mr. Pasic, could that person possibly have shared a room with you or accompanied you when you apparently were in Sarajevo in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is repeat what I've mentioned before. I know that hotel, Holiday Inn. I know what type of a hotel that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, that was not my question. My question was whether any person by the name of Dejanovic could have possibly accompanied you at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That person could have been with me but I don't think that person was sharing the same room with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Now, what position did that person by the name of Dejanovic, and it seems that you have one of the two you know in mind, what position did he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said to you, there were two men Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you certainly had one in your mind when you said that a person could have accompanied you, I take it, or could both have accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say either way. All I know that there were two of them. One was a member of the municipal board --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the other was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other one was the president of the municipal SDS board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So both candidates for accompanying you at that moment. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to refer Your Honours to tab 42, the -- page 23, the lower, the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you don't have to refer to the document, Mr. Pasic, because I'm going to ask you a question if this refreshes your recollection at all or if you were aware of this. At the 27th -- on the 27th of March 1992, at the assembly session, Dr. Karadzic said, and I quote, "When you return to your municipalities, especially the newly formed municipalities, I ask you to do what you are required and entitled to do under the law. The moment you arrive in your municipalities you must urgently establish Crisis Staffs." Does that in any way assist you in remembering why the Crisis Staff was formed in early April and on what basis it was formed in early April as described in your report on the work of the Crisis Staff? If not, just say so.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I have been speaking about the reasons why the Crisis Staff had not been set up earlier in Novi Grad. There was no need. It was only once the temperature rose, as it were, once tensions were exacerbated and political safety was jeopardised that the Crisis Staff was formed as the report claims in mid-April or around that time. I still don't know the date. I must say this again. I don't remember the meetings in Sarajevo, and it is quite obvious that we did not follow these instructions stated here. I'm not sure if that was a good thing or a bad thing but that's how it was. What this means is that we did not react immediately to these instructions given by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon before we proceed, at tab 40, the Holiday Inn receipts need a number, I take it. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1024, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you please sort out that we get the originals of both the receipts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you could turn your attention, Mr. Pasic, to the document that is marked Defence Exhibit 115, the report on the work of the Crisis Staff? I'm going to read you a part of this document, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For Your Honour's benefit I'm referring to page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And let me just read this to you rather than try to locate it for you Mr. Pasic in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Referring to the first complete paragraph at the top of page 7, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "With a slight delay the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had forwarded instructions for the work of municipal Crisis Staffs. Our municipality received the instructions on 20 May, and in accordance with the instructions we immediately approached the reorganisation of the Crisis Staff. In war conditions, Crisis Staff takes over all prerogatives and functions of the municipal assembly as for as long as it is unable to convene." And it goes on further to describe certain duties. Let me direct your attention, Mr. Pasic, first of all, to tab 41. Tab 41 needs a number, an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, it does not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: According to your own list, it doesn't, but -- oh, 41, let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed it does not need a number. There is a number on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's already twice in evidence, from what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I provide that shortly to the Court, Your Honour, the number that is being looked up at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's P65 Treanor 11, tabs 1, 2, 3 and P529, tab 76. That indeed was the Registrar. I take it reliably tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if you take a look at the document that is before you, this is a document that is signed or from Prime Minister Djeric. It discusses -- it's instructions, and it is dated April the 26th, 1992. Are these the instructions that you are referring to in the passage that I read to you, the instructions that you received on the 20th of May to form a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really, really can't remember. This may well be the case. If I had time to go through the whole document maybe that would refresh my memory but I really can't say whether this gave rise to any further instructions. Based on just this, I'm really unable to remember. I had a fleeting look at the instruction. I think this is called an excerpt from the instructions for the operation of Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in municipalities. If you give me sufficient time to go through these instructions, then we can backtrack, as it were and see if this is the thing we are talking about or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you take a look at item number 6 in the document, that reads, "The operation of the Crisis Staffs shall be based on constitutional and legal provisions and also on the decisions of the assembly, the Presidency, and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." If you refer to your report on the work of the Crisis Staffs, I will quote from a passage in that report. And I'm referring Your Honours to page 7 the penultimate paragraph, the second-to-last sentence starting with, "It found its work on constitutional and legal solutions and decisions of the assembly, Presidency and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Following its reorganisation, the Crisis Staff endeavoured to act according to the mentioned instruction." Does this assist you in --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can still say only this. I'm not trying to deny the substance of these instructions or the fact that they existed, but there is an open possibility that there were additional instructions in addition to this one. This is not something that I can talk about. I can't say that the Crisis Staff was ran -- was run and operated along the lines and guidelines provided by these instructions. I can't firmly state that. I am not trying to deny it but I'm not in a position to state in no uncertain terms, with sure and certain knowledge, that this was the only document in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- we'll move on, Mr. Pasic. In your report on the Crisis Staff, you assert in your report that the Crisis Staff works on constitutional and legal solutions and decisions of the assembly and the Presidency and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my personal report. It's a report produced by the Crisis Staff. It must be the way it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And this is a report, as you showed us in your tab 2, was a report that was adopted by the municipal assembly, correct? At a municipal assembly session on the 16th of July, this report was accepted by the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we failed to understand each other. If I got the interpretation right you said this was my report. This is not my report. This report was produced by the Crisis Staff. It was on behalf of the Crisis Staff that I signed the report but I was not the only person constituting the Crisis Staff. I'm not sure if I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This report that was signed by you and submitted to the municipal assembly was accepted by the municipal assembly with the assertions that are contained in it, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was accepted. That is clear enough if you look at the conclusions that we have reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me then focus on the last sentence of the passage I've just read, "the Crisis Staff endeavoured to act according to this instruction." In other words, I interpret that, and I want your comment on this, Mr. Pasic, I interpret this last sentence to mean that the Crisis Staff operated on the decisions of the assembly, you acted in respect of those, to implement those, decisions of the Presidency, and decisions of the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you read the last sentence, to this instruction. It reads, in my version, in the provisional translation, the mentioned instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, well, I can rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, especially I'm putting this to you in the English version five and a half lines above the list of nine names, you'll find language which you may understand could cause some confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After the Crisis Staff was reorganised, Mr. Pasic, the Crisis Staff endeavoured to act according to the mentioned instruction. Now, let me put this proposition to you, Mr. Pasic. The Crisis Staff endeavoured to work and follow the decisions of the assembly, the decisions of the Presidency, and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly it's a general one. You asked me whether it acted in accordance with these decisions of the Republika Srpska assembly and other bodies and authorities. I have already mentioned in my testimony that the Crisis Staff had no choice and could not have undertaken anything else. It was powerless to all practical intents and I think the same answer would apply to the question you've just asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Pasic, I want to change the subject. This Trial Chamber in the course of this trial has heard considerable evidence that Serbs, prior to the commencement of the war in April of 1992, that the JNA and the SDS party provided arms to Serb citizens within their communities. What can you tell us about that in respect of the municipality of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already spoken about that too. You can't say that there was a single source for all the population, in terms of obtaining weapons. There were several different sources for both Serbs and Muslims. One of them was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, what can you tell us about the JNA and the SDS providing weapons to Serbs in your community before the start of the war in April 1992. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, before April, I was not aware of any weapons being handed out. You should really be more specific and name some specific cases of weapons being handed out to people. I had no information to indicate that any of the official JNA bodies were supplying weapons to people. I was aware of that source too existing but not officially. It was through certain channels, certain officers, who were familiar with certain other people or friendly and they gave people weapons, but I'm not aware of any specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of the JNA and the SDS providing weapons to citizens in -- Serb citizens in your community prior to the beginning of the war in April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the witness just explained to us that he knew about JNA officers but that it was not official JNA activity. In your next question you ask whether the witness is aware of the JNA and the SDS. I think we should clearly identify what your question is about. Are you talking about those who served in the JNA or is your question about the JNA as a military organisation providing arms? So the distinction this witness has made should be clear in your question what you had in mind, or both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- I'd ask the witness to tell us what he knew about that, and I'm going to show you two documents that I'm going to ask you to comment on these documents, Mr. Pasic. If I could refer your attention first of all to tab 3. This is -- tab 3's exhibit number is P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I want to direct your attention to page 5 in the B/C/S of this document. This document is a document that was a military secret. It is a -- conclusions of the evaluation of the situation in Bosnia in the zone of the military -- of the 2nd district, and it is signed by General Kukanjac, and if you take a look at subpart 5, it deals with volunteer units in the zone of the 2nd military district. It references in subpart B -- do you have that in front of you, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be on page 4 where it starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 4, beginning of page -- top of page 5. This is a portion, Mr. Pasic, that reads, "The volunteer units in the zone of the 2nd Military District." You'll find it at the bottom of page 4 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the title?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. That's the title. This deals -- this report -- this report deals with the number of people who were volunteers within the 2nd Military District, and under subpart B it says there are 69198 people. In subpart C, Mr. Pasic, it says that the volunteer units are not part of the formation of the JNA or the Territorial Defence. And in subpart F, Mr. Pasic, it says that the JNA distributed 51900 pieces of armament, 75 per cent, and the SDS distributed 17298 pieces. Mr. Pasic, if I could then ask you to turn to tab 4, there is a bundle which is an addendum to Mr. Kukanjac's, General Kukanjac's report, and if I could direct your attention to the right-hand column, number 72, it refers to 1.000 men in Bosanski Novi. Now, Mr. Pasic, it has been our submission to this Court, when you tally up the number of men on this particular page, it matches with the number of weapons that are described in General Kukanjac's report. So from these two documents, it appears, Mr. Pasic, that 1.000 men in Bosanski Novi received weapons, either from the JNA or from the SDS or from both. Do you know anything about that? This document -- one more fact. This document is dated in March, Mr. Pasic, March of 1992. Now, do you know anything about the supply of weapons? Does this refresh your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document. As I've said before, there were several sources from which the weapons came. I'm not familiar with this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you -- the sources of weapons for the Serbs in your community prior to the beginning of the war, what were the sources?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, those weapons had come from military units, in several different ways. I'll tell you about some I know of. It's no secret that back in 1991, I think I've said this, there had been a mobilisation in Novi Grad municipality and that Serbs responded. I'm not sure how it was establishment-wise but I think one or two battalions had been mobilised in Croatian territory, and it was precisely those people. In a way, they had been ordered to do that, but according to some of the information that I had, they brought in some of the weapons and that may have been part of it. I can't say for sure but that may have been part of it because those were weapons belonging to the former JNA. So that may have been one of the sources, and if it is true, indeed, as you suggest, that Mr. Kukanjac said or wrote this, this might be somewhere in the military files recorded as this or that sort of equipment. I think establishment wise there were one or two battalions back in 1991 that had been mobilised. There remained in action or active throughout 1991 and 1992. They would come and go and that sort of reminds me of one of the possible sources. I have to say that there was a great deal of smuggling too, both Serbs and Muslims purchased their weapons. This was done on both sides, as I've pointed out before. People used their own private channels, specifically JNA officers were used as sources and the JNA comprised both Muslims and Serbs, as you know, so people used private channels to obtain weapons. Serbs gave weapons to Serbs and Muslims on the inside, as it were, gave weapons to other Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict in Bosanski Novi, we have heard evidence from witnesses in this Court that the helicopters landed in Serb villages in the Japra valley, and delivered arms. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I don't know that anyone had brought in weapons by helicopters but this is a purely subjective position. It's my own personal view. It must have been possible to bring in the weapons by land. I have never heard of a helicopter bringing weapons into Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you had a role in organising the Territorial Defence in Novi Grad, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were legal provisions governing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you had nothing to do with the organisation of the TO?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no need for me to be involved. The TO was there. I did say today or yesterday that the command structure comprised professionals. It existed before the war and continued to operate throughout the war. Only the soldiers were mobilised into the TO, but the commanding structure was composed of professionals that operated in both peace and wartime. There were legal provisions governing there entire mechanism. It wasn't down to a decision that I might have made or somebody else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to turn to tab 5 of the bundle in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm directing the court's attention to -- in English, to the last paragraph in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I direct you, Mr. Pasic, to the last paragraph of the document. Let me read this passage to you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document, Your Honours, that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor from the CSB building in Banja Luka in February of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Citizens of Serbian ethnicity are organised within the system of Territorial Defence, mainly through the efforts of Radomir Pasic, president of the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly. So far, about 1300 Serbs have been armed, mostly with automatic infantry weapons, and they control a considerable amount of equipment for anti-armour combat, 90-millimetre launchers, one; 76-millimetre Pack Howitzer gun and a smaller amount of 82- and 120-millimetre mortars." This document is a review of the security of relevant information for Bosanski Novi municipality. Let me ask you again, Mr. Pasic: Did you have a role in organising the system of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is repeat the answer I gave previously. I don't know who wrote this and on the basis of what. I don't know what they considered to be my contribution to this. Let me repeat that there was no need for me to get involved in the establishment of the TO Staff. It existed before I became the president of municipality, and it continued to operate regardless of my activities, and in this text, I don't see what is attributed to me when it comes to the arming. I don't know who wrote this text, who the author is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- Mr. Pasic, in terms of the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence, can you describe for us the chain of command in the Territorial Defence? Identify the commander of the Territorial Defence? First of all, can you identify him by name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before, and I can repeat it, Damjanovic, Mile, was the commander of the TO staff. The chief of the TO staff was rad Slav Sekulic, sorry, Radislav.
