As for the other posts and formations, I don't know. I know that there was some formations. These two men were the key persons when it comes to the operation of the TO staff. They had their assistants. As for the exact titles of these men, I'm not sure about that, but that can be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mile Damjanovic is referred to in your report to the -- the work on the Crisis Staff. He was indeed a member of the Crisis Staff, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As is written in this Crisis Staff report, people were members of the Crisis Staff ex officio, and this is something that this report confirms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who were the superiors of the commanders of the Crisis Staff -- of the Territorial Defence in April and May?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who were superiors to this Crisis Staff leadership? Who were Mile Damjanovic's superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, who were their superiors? The commanders of the Territorial Defence in Bosanski Novi, what was the chain of command? Did they respond to the Crisis Staff? Did the Crisis Staff give them orders and instructions, or did somebody else give them orders and instructions? And if so, who?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said this and I will repeat. The Crisis Staff did have no powers over the TO staff command. Even though they used in some documents the word "orders", in actuality the Crisis Staff had no such powers. Initially, in the very beginning, I think that the command was at the level of the republic. I don't know who specifically was superior to the TO staff command. I don't know the exact person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You say in the beginning. What time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean all the way up to May, until the army of Republika Srpska was established. This was the time when the JNA disintegrated so there was a vacuum left. In that period of time they attempted to set up the army of Republika Srpska. I don't know how long this period lasted, and during this vacuum, I'm not sure who the TO staff was responsible to. I don't know whether this automatically was transferred to the army of Republika Srpska or to somebody else. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question but not until after a number has been assigned to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say I'm certainly going to put the Prosecution to proof again on provenance on this. I'm going to object to its admissibility, and I'm raise to raise why it hasn't been disclosed under Rule 68. It's entirely a matter for Your Honours as to when I should commence owes arguments, but I'm going to take all those points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- you would say that the provenance should have been disclosed of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm saying it should have been disclosed under Rule 68 firstly, then I'm going to ask proof, exact proof as to where it came from, and then I'm going to -- depending on the answer to those various questions I'm going to object to its admissibility as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. Nevertheless, I think as a matter of fact it has been assigned a number already or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, this is not a decision on admission but just an administrative matter that provisionally a number is assigned to this document. No decision has yet been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got no problem with that, of course, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 5 will be P0125 and the English translation 1025.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to understand this is already been mentioned this morning. I would like to understand -- you told us that the JNA had withdrawn to go towards the border, the Croatian border. And I had understood that it had been replaced by what you have called the VRS, and a while ago I thought I understood you had said there had been a vacuum, a period of time during which there was no army on the territory of your municipality. Have I understood you properly and how long did this interruption last where there were forces of the TO and these paramilitary groups which you mentioned this morning? I would like to understand -- maybe am I too curious, but I would like to understand the situation, the precise military situation on the ground. Was there a period during which there was no army as such? I make a difference between an army and the Territorial Defence forces and the paramilitaries. Could you answer this question? Or just tell us if you can't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer that. I know about this. First of all, I don't think you understood me well, if I understood your question correctly. Because it was lengthy. In my previous testimony I said that sometime in May, I'm not sure about the date, the JNA withdrew to the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia but not to Croatia as has been interpreted to me. So the JNA did not go to the border with Croatia but rather to the border with today's Serbia and Montenegro. I repeat, I don't know the exact date but it was in May. I think it was May when the JNA left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina for good. The TO was an integral component of the JNA and it needs to be distinguished from the paramilitary formations. TO and the JNA were legal formations established by law. As for the paramilitary formations, as the term indicates, they existed outside of the law. Nobody officially established them. Nobody stood behind them. These were just people who got organised in order to commit crimes and to disturb law and order in the territory of the entire Bosnia one could say although I'm here to testify only about Novi Grad. I repeat, I think that this vacuum was -- did not exist for a long period of time, and it lasted precisely from the moment when the JNA left the territory until the VRS was officially established. Once again, I do not know the exact date. I think it was in late June. We could see in the conclusion of the municipal assembly when they asked for a battalion to be established. I think that such battalions were established in late June, early July, which means that there was a period of time when formally the army did exist. I think that the decision was reached in Banja Luka on the 11th, 12th, or 13th of May. I wasn't present when it was done. On the ground, however, the army did not start functioning right away. And during that period of time, the TO staff represented the army. So this is what I described as a vacuum. During this period of time, there was no real army on the ground, and this was from the moment the JNA left until the army was officially established in late June, early July, when the actual battalions were established, battalions of the VRS, in the territory of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to complete my question. I would like to know if -- I would like to know whether this TO had heavy weapons or not, or -- by heavy weapons, I mean mortars, guns, cannons, not only rifles or light weapons. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, I think that this is called light infantry weapons. I don't know about the calibres. Since I'm not an officer, I'm not a military person, I can't be fully certain about this. I think that they had some mortars. I wouldn't be able to tell you more about calibres. So they had more than just rifles, they had some mortars and some machine-guns. I think that military experts would be better placed to explain this to you, namely what exactly the term "light infantry weapons" covers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The report says that on the 11th of May, armed conflict started on the town territory, infantry and artillery fire directed towards the town lasted for three hours. Had the JNA already withdrawn when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to repeat that in Novi Grad municipality, there was one barracks but I think that it only had reserve of soldiers there, not active-duty personnel. In that period of time, in Novi Grad, there was no JNA army. It is possible that the army was present on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period of time. However, in Novi Grad municipality, I think that there was no longer any JNA at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. -- Mr. Harmon, two judges interrupted your line of questioning. We need to have a break soon. If this would be a suitable moment, we'll have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until ten minutes to six and I'd like to deal for a couple of minutes only with some procedural matters when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will first deal with a few procedural matters. First of all, the Chamber has delivered a written decision in relation to what I would call the Davidovic issue. Second, one of the matters that have not been discussed but is certainly not -- certainly -- is certainly does still cause great concern is the 65 ter summaries, the preparation and the communication of information to the Prosecution. We find no time to discuss it at this moment but the -- since the concern is still fully there, the Defence is at least invited to see whether, over the recess and the time when we are not sitting, whether it can improve its performance and then we'll see after the recess what the situation is and whether it will need further attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If it's any consolation I would have urged the Court to put off the matter today at any rate because Mr. Stewart indicated some week or so ago he was personally anxious to deal with that matter. Of course, I will convey to the Court [sic] what Your Honour has said. We hope that the next few weeks will help us sort these matters out. That's all I can helpfully, I hope, helpfully say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a matter I will raise at a later stage why it's not possible for us at this moment to pay any further attention to the matter. So I will continue with some other procedural matters. On the 22nd of November, the Chamber has requested the Prosecution to respond to a number of Defence exhibits introduced through witness Vasic. The exhibit numbers are D70, D72, 73, 74, 76, 77, 79, and D81, up to and including 82G. That's day 81 up to and including 81G. Then D85, D86, D87, and D88. As of today, the Prosecution has raised no objection against these documents and therefore the Chamber admits the exhibits mentioned above into evidence. The Chamber also notes that a number of documents introduced by both parties are yet to receive translation. The Prosecution exhibits that require translation are P954, P968 to P973, P976 to P978, P992, and P1008. The Defence exhibits that require translation are D78, D80, D82(H), D82(I), D83, D92 to D98, D99(A) to D99V, D100 to D102, and D105 to D108. The Chamber requests the parties to provide translations for the documents mentioned above not later than by the 15th of January unless good cause is shown. In addition, two of the Prosecution exhibits, namely P1012 and P1013, admitted into evidence by the Chamber on the 24th of November, are undated. There is no reference to any context in terms of time. The Trial Chamber requests the Prosecution to provide the dates or at least to provide any indication, even if it's not an exact date, for the documents mentioned above, no later than the 15th of January. Otherwise, the Chamber may reconsider the admission of these exhibits. Finally, the Chamber requests the Prosecution to verify the accuracy of the translations of certain text portions from the following exhibits: P851, which is the transcript of the video interviews with Mr. Krajisnik dated the 25th of November and the 17th of December 1992; P852, which is the interview with Mr. Krajisnik dated the 21st of December 1992; and P877.A which is the transcript of the video of the funeral in Vlasenica dated the 30th of December 1992. The specific portion that is need special attention are in an attachment provided with the copy of the handout of these -- of these observations which will be distributed to the parties. The highlighted parts in the attachment require careful translation. These are the procedural matters. You're informed, I hope, or perhaps I should have told you that everything would be distributed to you so that you didn't have to write it all down. Then we could continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do need to mention one matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The indignation that I expressed earlier in relation to tab 5 was, I regret to say from my only personal point of view, completely unfounded. Mr. Harmon has told me that tab 5 apparently has been disclosed to the Defence on no less than four occasions, twice in 2001, once in 2002, and once in 2004. I apologise unreservedly to my learned friend and his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the apologies are accepted, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time, you told us something about the provenance of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to challenge it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, then, on the record as well. Then the witness could be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very briefly before he is escorted in, Your Honour, I had one issue I would like to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is arriving, it doesn't matter I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's if there is any tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If there is tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the end of the day. I know there will be an end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I want to follow up on a question posed to you by the judge and I want a very clear answer if you're able to give one. Did the Territorial Defence in Bosanski Novi possess artillery weapons in the time period we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that one already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. There is a difference between mortars -- I want to put aside mortars. Did they possess artillery weapons to your knowledge during the time period of the events that you have testified about in the Japra valley in May and June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the witness has told us that he's not a military expert and that he has already difficulties in understanding what light artillery is. Could you please explain to the witness what you mean by artillery weapons so that he has a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't want to spend a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not asking to you spend a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness told us he had served his mandatory service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What part of the JNA did you serve your time in? What unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a signals officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do you know -- you know what a mortar is?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You know what an artillery piece is, a cannon, 75-millimetre cannon, other types of -- 120-millimetre cannons? Do you know those types of weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm roughly familiar with the existence of something they call light artillery and heavy artillery but I would not interpret the distinction itself simply because I have no professional experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the TO have heavy artillery at its disposal in the time period we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see you are quite persistent, but I must repeat my previous answer, and please don't get me wrong. What I believe is that they had light infantry weapons as I have already described. I am not sure what that implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different topic because I have a limited amount of time, Mr. Pasic. I want to talk about the police patrol incident that you described took place on the 10th and the 11th of May 1992. Your testimony to us yesterday was that on the night between the 10th and the 11th, of May, a military police patrol was shot at while passing the village of Blagaj. You attempted to calm down the situation on the 11th of May. The situation -- shooting started again, and went into the second night. Now I want to ask you, Mr. Pasic, are you aware that the Muslims on the 11th of May attempted to put a roadblock up into the village of Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, or the reports I received, this was not an obstacle. There was fire by infantry weapons against a military police vehicle. I think I said so yesterday. Two military policemen were slightly wounded on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I asked you if you aware after that incident the Muslims in the village of Blagaj Japra attempted to put up a roadblock to block the road in the village of Blagaj? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything like that. This is the main road leading from Novi Grad to Prijedor, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question simply was whether you were aware of a roadblock being erected. The answer "no" is fine. Where that road leads to, whether you are aware of other things, is not in the question. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me refer Your Honours to tab 6. This needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 6, Your Honours, will be P1026.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to paragraph 3 in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For your information, Mr. Pasic, this is a document from the 5th Corps command of the JNA signed by General Talic. It's dated the 11th of May. It's addressed to the 2nd Military District. And let me read to you paragraph 3. A second -- starting with the second sentence: "In the municipality of Bosanski Novi, an attempt to block the road in the village of Blagaj has been made by SDA members. The command of the Prijedor garrison has intervened and the military police have set up a checkpoint there." Now, Mr. Pasic, this refers to the Prijedor garrison of the JNA operating on your territory on the 11th of May 1992. Does that refresh your recollection as to when the JNA was still operating on your territory?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember. I said that it was about this time that the JNA withdrew but I can say when specifically. I'm not familiar with the fact that there was this roadblock in the village of Blagaj. At least I was not aware of it. I don't know that this garrison was active and operational. Whoever wrote this, Talic or whoever else, I'm entirely unsure what they were trying to imply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you could just have answered by saying this does not refresh my recollection. Because you start repeating all of the evidence you gave earlier and add to that that what you -- in addition to what you said, you already did not know, you add to that. If you just listen to the question, this does not refresh your recollection. It doesn't tell you anything more than you had told us already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, on the 11th of May, didn't the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence conduct a mortar attack on the village of Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the report indicates, that, as they say, there was a warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me refer you to tab number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the report says, at least if we are talking about the report on the activities of the -- it says that on the 11th, there was a -- from what I remember, an attack on the town, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a difference, Your Honour, between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if you please assist me in -- that's in the beginning, perhaps, and then perhaps later on, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's on the bottom of page 4 of the English version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question was directed toward Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Turn your attention -- Your Honour' attention and the witness's attention to tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, I'm directing your attention to page 2 of the English version under the caption, "Bosanski Novi."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, witness, this -- I direct your attention in the B/C/S version to the portion that is at the bottom -- bottom third of the page if says, "Bosanski Novi." This is a Security Service Centre Banja Luka report to the Serbian Republic of BiH MUP and to the SJB and to all Chief of Staff. It's an information from May the 11th and May the 12th, and if we turn to the section dealing with Bosanski Novi, this says, and I'm referring to the third line, the sentence that reads as follows: "Members of the Muslim nationality put up a barricade in Blagaj village and members of the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence carried out a mortar attack on the village at 2100 hours." What can you tell us about that, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagaj is not only on one side of the river Sana but also on the other. It straddles the river, in other words. I said I knew nothing about the roadblock across the main road and I think that's what causes the confusion to arise. But there is Blagaj, there is Japraj [phoen] and there is Blagaj Rijeka. The exact location is not specified. This is one village. But that's the internal distinction so to speak. On the other side of the road to the upper villages, there were roadblocks, or barricades but that's precisely what I was trying to draw the distinction between the main road and the other road, where the roadblock was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I take it from your answer, Mr. Pasic, you are unable to assist us and this Trial Chamber in respect of the mortar attack that was carried out on Blagaj by the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence. Do I understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've referred to this report a number of times. It was the night between the 10th and 11th of November. And I told you what happened. I can only repeat what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have read the -- you've heard the passage I referred to, Mr. Pasic. I would like you to comment, if you can, if you can tell us what you know, about the mortar attack that was conducted on the village of Blagaj at 2100 hours by Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I have been talking about, this attack. I think the incidents occurred at around 11.00 or 12.00, I don't know exactly because I know it was past midnight when I received a phone call from the TO Command Staff. They phoned me because I was at home. That's why I was saying that Mr. Muhamedagic and I arrived together at the staff command which was in Novi Grad, the town, itself, whereas this other place is about eight or nine kilometres from the town, away from the town. I wasn't up there when the incident occurred and I can only say what I've already said, and which is indicated by the Crisis Staff report, and what the command said after all. They fired warning mines or missiles warning shells, probably that was a reference to a mortars, so that is the sort of infantry weapon that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that you were informed by the Territorial Defence that they had fired warning mortars into the village of Blagaj? Do I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That night, I was informed that a TO staff, military police patrol, had been fired at in the village of Blagaj, and that two military policemen had been wounded on the occasion. That was what I was told that night, and that's why I went straight to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking you about what you know about the Bosanski Novi TO, following the attack on the police patrol, firing mortars into the village of Blagaj village. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that at least two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well perhaps I didn't understand. Would you mind repeating what you know about mortars being fired into the Blagaj village on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is precisely this report by the Crisis Staff that indicates this. Warning mines were fired. If I remember correctly, no specific buildings were targeted. This was by way of a warning that these missiles were fired. No specific people or buildings were targeted. These were fired in a general direction because there are meadows there, and forests too. At least that was the information that I had. I'm telling you about what I know and that's what it says in the report, that warning mines or mortars were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you give the order to fire those mortars and those warning shots?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't listen carefully, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you answer my question? Did you give the order to fire those warning shots?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 8 -- I'm sorry, tab 7 needs an exhibit number, still?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P1027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 8 which also needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1028, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, this is a report from the Croatian authorities who were monitoring the situation in Bosanski Novi. This report is based on intercepted communications, and I refer you and the Court to the second paragraph starting with "the JA police patrol from Bosanski Novi was attacked by ambush at 2315 hours in the area of the village of Blagaj. It was attacked by infantry arms and one Zolja hand-held rocket launcher shell was fired. Two police members were wounded so that JA," that means the Yugoslav army, "brought three tanks in front of the barricade and issued an ultimatum to surrender. At 1840 hours, Major Zeljaja informed Colonel Devic who forwarded the information to the general that the following event took place in Blagaj. According to the order of the president of Bosanski Novi municipality, the Serbs opened fire at Muslim villages from artillery and mortars. That was not necessary because the measures had already been taken. Everyone had been disarmed and everything had been mopped up or cleansed. They are completely crazy extremists led by the municipality president." Let me ask you again, Mr. Pasic: Did you give the order to open fire on Muslim villages with artillery and mortars on the 11th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am going to require some more details about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is certainly not a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will be glad to provide the foundation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in the days that followed this attack on the village of Blagaj with mortar rounds, the situation calmed down and there was no additional armed conflict in your municipality, was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand which date you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Following the mortar attack on the village of Blagaj on the 11th of May 1992, thereafter, the situation remained tense but there was no additional conflict in your municipality, was there? I'm talking in the days that followed.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I said in my previous answer, isn't it? There was a lull but it only lasted until the afternoon the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you told us about the lull, there was some fighting and then after that, there was -- there was no additional combat in your municipality through, say, the following three or four days, was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just can't say that it was like that. I'm telling you this was between the 10th and the 11th, and then this went on for the next 10 days or thereabouts. There were certain disturbances, there was firing, and what I just talked about, when we talked about the Crisis Staff report. I told you that on the 11th, on the morning of the 11th, there was a lull but for reasons unknown to me there was again firing in the afternoon of the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the next exhibit, which is found in tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs an exhibit number as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring Your Honours to the English version to paragraph 3 of the report. This is a JNA 5th Corps command report dated the 15th of May 1992 to the command of the 2nd Military District. It's a regular combat report. It's signed by a Major General Talic, who was the commander. And in the -- it reads, I'll start second sentence, "In the area of responsibility of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation is still complex, especially in" -- and then it mentions Bosanski Novi. "There have been no armed conflicts in this territory but the situation is extremely tense."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does that help you remember more clearly, Mr. Pasic, about the days that followed the attack on the village of Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to focus your attention on a different subject, then, Mr. Pasic. And that is on the attacks on the Muslim villages in the Japra valley that took place on the 23rd or the 24th of May 1992. This Trial Chamber has heard considerable evidence about what happened in the Japra valley, reports of people who lived in those villages, describing being forced out of their villages because their villages were bombarded, houses being burned, their mosques being destroyed, and their being forced to move out of their villages. Now, I believe that you have -- you would agree with that, wouldn't you, Mr. Pasic? That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in my previous testimony. There was disturbance and there were clashes in the Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let's -- I want to turn your attention to tab 11. And tab 11 already has an exhibit number. It's P892, Brown, tab 50. This is a report that is dated the 15th of August 1992, and it is a report on -- for the security station in Bosanski Novi, and it describes in the English version, under -- at page 1, the bottom of page 1, under reception centres in the area of Bosanski Novi municipality, in this document, Mr. Pasic, it describes combat activities, several combat activities toward the areas and villages with majority Muslim inhabitants -- I'm sorry, let me start again. It describes -- I'll -- the night of 10-11 May 1992, in the place of Blagaj Rijeka, according to the reports of members of military police patrol, military police, they -- military policemen were attacked. These events caused several combat activities toward the areas and villages with majority of Muslim inhabitants. So on 24 May 1992, all inhabitants from the villages from the area of the upper valley of Japra river were accommodated in the central part of Blagaj Japra. After a funeral of a member of military police who got killed on the occasion of the attack on Prijedor in the town settlement of Prekosanje combat activities occurred in the evening hours of 1 June 1992. All aforementioned combat activities from performed by armed and uniformed persons who were self-organised, or members of Territorial Defence, or military units of the JNA. Members of the public security station Bosanski Novi did not participate in the aforementioned activities. Now, if we turn in that same document to an additional description that is provided, it's on page 4, additional description that's provided of the attack in the villages in the Japra valley, Mr. Pasic, I'll read to you the following passage. "According to the information of this public security station, very intensive and unselective artillery fire from many arms was opened in the wider area of the valley Japra river, villages, Blagaj, Japra, Maslovare, Crna Rijeka, Suhaca, Hozic, and Donji Agici, in the night of 23-24 May and on 24 May 1992." This describes in the night of the 23 to the 24th of May and in the day of the 24th of May, Mr. Pasic, seven separate Muslim villages being attacked by heavy artillery fire. What do you know about that, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this is contained in this report, and this was precisely the reason for the negotiations that I spoke about. I didn't understand well something that you read out on page of this report. At least the report reads different from what was interpreted to me. All of the above-mentioned combat operations were conducted by the armed uniformed persons who were self-organised or members of the TO units or JNA war units. Because that's what the text says. It says "or" which means that this is just an assumption on their part, and that really coincides with what I said. People did wear uniforms but they were not under the TO Staff, which at the time was part of the regular army in that territory. Based on the information of the police station, who wrote this report, there were uniformed people but these people did not constitute an official, regular unit, which was supposed to be under the TO Staff command. This is something that I said in my statement as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the "or, or" matter. Again that was on page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's on the bottom of page 1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says in English as well, "or, or" so we now heard the comment of the witness. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence in this Tribunal, Mr. Pasic, that artillery fire opened on seven separate villages in the Japra valley on the night of the 23rd and the 24th of May, was conducted by some paramilitary units, the small paramilitary units that you described in your testimony earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when describing the artillery attacks, we said enough. There is no need for me to go into more detail. The report says that certain groups, and I even emphasised this, that some members of the sector staff, I said this, this morning, people who were in charge of that area, Krslje, Mala Novska, and Agici, they refused the order which came from the TO Staff command about not shooting. This is what is stated in this report. It is quite clear. It's not vague at all. It is clear that there were certain individuals, certain small groups, and also some individuals who were members of the sector staff and regional staff who acted outside of the TO staff instructions. This information came from the public security station in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The people in the Japra valley were forcibly expelled from their villages as a result of that artillery fire that was directed toward their villages; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained that as well in the report. I said that people from these villages in the course of these clashes, came to the village of Blagaj, and this is where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They were expelled from their villages as a result of that fire that was directed at their villages. That's what you say in your report, Mr. Pasic, on page 8 of your report. In the middle of the page, you say, "armed activities which included the use of mortars caused expulsion of Muslim civilians from the villages of Donji Agici, Celopek, Hozic, Suhaca and they were taken to the settlement of Blagaj. Your report uses the word "expelled." I don't want to get into a semantics debate with you. Now, Mr. Pasic, given that you were certain that very serious crimes had been committed against members of your community, the Muslim community, did you report what had happened to the leadership in the ARK? Did you have conversations with people in the ARK leadership what had happened in your community? If so, with whom and when?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Did I inform whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Kupresanin, and other leaders in the ARK region about what had happened in your community?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I talked to Mr. Brdjanin or not. The AR Krajina was not really a legal institution. It was more only -- it existed more on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you're not invited to give your views on what the ARK was but you were just asked whether you reported and you said you don't remember whether you talked to Mr. Brdjanin. Now, the question included Mr. Kupresanin and other leaders in the ARK region. So would you please answer that question, whether you had conversations with them on what had happened in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was discussed but I don't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did you discuss it with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular issue, I don't know when exactly I discussed it. I think that -- I think, I'm not sure, that we informed, once, Mr. Kupresanin about the situation, without any further details, because at the time they were powerless to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that conversation with Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I just told you, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you talk to anybody at the republic level leadership about what had happened in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I didn't talk then, during that critical period of time, because I believe that there was no communication with other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that, where all the leadership was. They were present in Sarajevo and Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, again, you say you think you didn't talk. You were asked about whether you did talk, and you said I didn't talk at that critical period. When, then, did you do that? You're invited to respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to come to his rescue, Your Honour, that in my respectful submission is an unfair interruption. Your Honour, with respect, he is answering the question there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was, did you talk to anybody at a republic level leadership about what had happened in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it was quite clear that he was being asked about Mr. Kupresanin and that particular period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand the question to be whether Mr. Pasic, but please correct me when I'm wrong, Mr. Harmon whether apart from speaking to ARK officials whether he talked to any republic-level, that's one level higher up, whether he discussed it with them. And then the witness started saying that he did not at that moment. So he's invited to tell us whether he did, and perhaps the question on when you did it might be the following one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sitting down to save time, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- and I also always will carefully listen to if any of the parties says that I'm unfairly treating a witness, that's -- you can be sure of that. So I'll give it further consideration. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, Mr. Pasic? At the time of these events did you talk to anybody at the republic level leadership about what was happening and what had happened in your community?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said previously that sometime, I don't know whether it was June or early July, I'm not sure, but I think it was that period of time, this is when I talked to Mr. Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic, if I remember well, and I believe that I've stated this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The question was at the time these events -- these events, did you talk to anybody in the republic leadership? Not talking about much later. At the time of these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the problem, which events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that we are talking about the mortar attack on --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Talking about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More that are attack on Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour I had moved to the subject of the attacks on the villages in the Japra valley on the 23rd and the 24th and we were discussing those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that's the time I was referring to, Mr. Pasic. At the time of the attacks on the villages, Muslim villages in the Japra valley on the 23rd and the 24th of May, did you speak to anybody at the republic leadership about what was happening at the time of those events?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's move on into your document, then, Mr. Pasic, this document that's -- D115. After the Muslims were sequestered, after they had been expelled from their villages in the Japra valley and they were sequestered in the village of Blagaj, according to your document, I'm referring to page 9 of the -- page 9 of Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D115.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we can refer to your document at page 9, the middle paragraph, I will read it to you, Mr. Pasic. Rather than have you take the time to read it, let me read it to you. It says, "The population of Blagaj remained without a solution so one was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know my learned friend is trying to save time but the problem is the witness then starts looking for the passage. He doesn't then listen to what he's being asked. I would much rather he found the passage. I know it takes time but it's only fair that the witness looks at the document when he's being asked a question like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, if I read it to him, perhaps he can find it, Your Honour, but I can't direct him to it. Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let me read there passage to you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Population in Blagaj remained without a solution, so one was requested for its migration. Negotiations were held with the organs of the autonomous region, with the government of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and UNPROFOR. The remaining possibility was to expedite a voluntary emigration toward Banja Luka and that a return to the valley of Japra was definitely impossible, but this population showed no willingness to it." My questions, Mr. Pasic, relate to the negotiations that you had with the organs of the autonomous region in respect of the emigration of these people. Who did you speak to in the ARK region? Who did you negotiate with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already talked about this. As far as I can remember, at least the only conversation that I remember is the one with Mr. Kupresanin. I talked to him. I don't know whether anybody else from the Crisis Staff talked to him. It is possible. However, after all this time, I cannot remember who and when talked to him. I do not wish to challenge this report now. There is no reason for that. But most likely there was somebody there from the AR Krajina government, and UNPROFOR. I remember talking to Mr. Kupresanin, but that conversation had the goal of informing him. That was the nature of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 10 of that same document, the paragraph -- second paragraph from the bottom. I'll read it to you then I'm going to ask you about it: "Along with this problem there remained the issue of Blagaj residents. Since the option of their emigration toward western Europe was definitely discarded, the superior bodies (AR Krajina government, government of Serb Republic, BH), et cetera, were asked to determine a decisive stand on the status of that Muslim population. The answer given was that there it was a possibility of them being exchanged for Serbs captured in Zenica, Travnik and Busovaca, but this was not -- this has not taken place." Two questions about that. With whom did you negotiate at the government of the Serb republic in respect of the status of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly about who I talked with in AR Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No I'm asking you about the government of the Serb Republic of BH. Who did you talk to in the Serb Republic of BH, as recorded in this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I repeat this for the third or fourth time: If you have in mind that critical period of time, the 23rd or the 24th, I believe I did not speak to anyone in the government of the Serb Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this report that was confirmed and ratified by the municipal assembly and accepted by it is in error? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I didn't say that was erroneous. I just said that I did not speak to anyone in the government of the Serb Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who for Bosanski Novi municipality spoke about the status of the Muslim population with a -- with members of the government of the Serb republic? Can you assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't remember whether anybody talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, the answer that is given was that -- one answer was that these people could be exchanged for Serbs. You know who gave that response?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that response. I believe that this information came from Banja Luka. I don't know from what official organs, though. It was presented as a possibility. They said there was a possibility to have some exchanges, at least that's what I was told. I was told that it is possible to have some Serb inhabitants who lived in the area where they were threatened exchanged for some other inhabitants. However, this was not implemented, not in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there anybody from the ARK region or the republic level of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who suggested that additional police forces could be sent to protect these people and protect them in their homes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was us who asked from the public security centre in Banja Luka. I think that it was us who asked for a special unit, which was located in Banja Luka. I don't know what period of time it was, but I know that this unit came to Novi Grad and it did more of a disservice to us than anything else, and I believe that this is reported somewhere in one of the reports. After that, when we realised that this special unit was really not helping us at all, we asked that it urgently be sent back because it really only did us a disservice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before you continue, I'm looking at the clock. I was informed that the Defence would need at least 15 minutes for re-examination. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that means that we cannot finish today. Then the next question would be -- there has been an allusion already to that at an earlier moment today, whether there will be any hearing tomorrow. For urgent personal reasons, I cannot sit tomorrow. The Rules give an opportunity to the other two judges to continue in my absence. I will consult with my colleagues whether they wish to continue in my absence or whether they rather wait until I'm present again, which would mean that, since tomorrow is the last day before the recess, that we would then have to invite the witness to come back after he has returned over the Christmas period. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't say the Chamber has decided but the two remaining judges, if I may deliver the decision of the two remaining judges, they will not use the opportunity given by Rule 15 bis, I think it is. They would prefer to hear the whole of the testimony of the witness with three judges, which means that in a couple of minutes we'll adjourn. And, Mr. Pasic, you may have followed what I just said. It has, as a consequence for you, that since we will not sit tomorrow and since tomorrow will be the last day before the Christmas recess, that the Chamber will ask you to come back, and then Mr. Josse and Mr. Harmon, I think it would be -- although the Chamber fully understands that this is not very pleasant for you, to leave The Hague and then to return after a couple of weeks, and the first day we are sitting again is the 16th of January. I do not know what has been prepared for the 16th of January, Mr. Josse, but could we -- I take it that we would need another -- all together another perhaps, together with the questions of the Bench, another two hours with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that's right. We need to schedule at least two hours because my estimate of 15 minutes was at the last break. Presently I intend a relatively long re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's say we need at least half a session because the judges might have some questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be -- for the 16th of January, would that cause you any problems? Because I don't think that we have received yet, but I'm not quite sure about that, a list of witnesses to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Court has not received a list of witnesses of the that's absolutely correct and we could schedule this witness for that day, as far as I'm concerned. I suppose my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Harmon the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, as you may have noticed, we were discussing the possibility of continuing your examination on the 16th of January. Would it be possible for you to come back on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret that we will be unable to finish tonight. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to take into consideration certain religious circumstances in my life. The 20th of January is a very important holiday for me. It's my patron saint day. So I need several days in order to prepare for the festivities. I am prepared to come back, but please take this into account and please take into account this event, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if we would not need any more than Monday, the 16th, what we -- let me just look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it may be a Tuesday, Your Honour, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a Monday for the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 16th of January, we are scheduled for the morning hours. So most likely, Mr. Pasic, there would be a possibility -- I'm not certain about flights, but most likely there would be an opportunity for you to return on that same day, so that three days would remain until the 20th of January. Would that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's very unlikely he could return that day, Your Honour. I think that's extremely unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I think - we could ask - he would fly from Zagreb and I think the only flight is the one in the middle of the day, 12.00-ish, I think. I don't pretend to be an expert on these things. Very far from it. Perhaps we could ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the -- Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has considered the matter. The witness is invited to come back on the 16th of January. And Mr. Pasic, we'll do whatever we can to see that you return as quickly as possible, if possible that same day. If not, then certainly the next day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be any change, you'll hear from the Victims and Witnesses section because they cannot be consulted at this very moment because of the time of the day. Then we'll adjourn until the 16th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, there was one matter --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- that I did want to raise with the court. It was in respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of the witness? Yes, you said you would like to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Pasic, first of all, you were talking about religion. A happy Christmas for you as well, even if it's perhaps not on the same day as we celebrate Christmas. A happy Christmas to you and your people, and we would like to see you back on the 16th at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you. You may follow Madam Usher, and I have to instruct you that even for these longer periods of time, you are instructed not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given and I can imagine that, since it was a public testimony, that people start asking questions about it or want to discuss it with you. You are instructed not to do so, and neither to discuss anything about the testimony still to come. Then I wish you a safe trip home for this moment and I would like to thank you for your flexibility and your willingness to come back on the 16th of January. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only wanted to raise one matter in respect of an exhibit. I'll do it very quickly. I was fearful that it would become too stale if we have to wait until January to raise this issue. I'm referring to Exhibit P967. This was a set of handwritten notes that related to the testimony of Mr. Stavnjak. The Court -- I had made a submission that these handwritten notes had been recovered in Gorazde - I'm referring to the transcript at page 18051 - that this -- Your Honour had asked me if I had further details. I said I would make a further inquiry, and I have made that inquiry, Your Honour, and these handwritten notes were recovered by a unit of the Bosnian army at a house in Gorazde in late August of 1992 after the Serb forces had withdrawn from Gorazde, and the house was the command of the Serb Territorial Defence forces. There was a command of the Serb Territorial Defence forces in the house where this document was recovered. That's what I wanted to submit to the Court. Thank you for your indulgence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's then on the record. If this raises any further concerns or comments from the Defence, we'll hear from you Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make it clear that Mr. Harmon was good enough to tell me that earlier. This was an inquiry of the Chamber rather than a point raised by Mr. Stewart who was dealing with that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, it could be that on the basis of this information he would have any additional concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In that case I will reserve the Defence position. I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will adjourn until the 16th of January but not until after I have -- unless there is anything else, Mr. Harmon, but not until after -- I have to stop. I just got a message that there might be a problem with the 16th. I think I already said to the witness that if there'll be any change, the 17th is suggested now but I'd like to mare more about these problems before we make any change. Then, of course, the parties will be informed and the witness will be informed. As I said, I'll not adjourn until after I have wished everyone good days, whether religious or just at the end of the year and the start of the new year. Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber is fully aware that celebrating Christmas in your position is not the thing one would wish. One would wish other circumstances. The Chamber is fully aware of that, but nevertheless we would like to convey also to you our best wishes for the coming weeks. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of January 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
